Image tdsc-cicloid:prof built with build-variant.sh; test suite 42/42 passed. Run 1: `bench.sh tdsc-cicloid:prof prof --users 20000 --seconds 120 --ramp 20` (the loadgen hold stretched to 180 s) with a driver that, inside the hold, collected a vernier wall profile (60 s, 500 us), a stackprof `:cpu` profile (25 s, 500 us ITIMER_PROF, raw) and a vernier wall+allocation profile (12 s, allocation_interval 25), `docker cp`'d each out before the container was removed; io_uring selector confirmed active (seccomp unconfined). Run 2 (prof2, 60 s hold): strace installed during ramp, `strace -c -f -p 1` for 20 s in the hold bracketed by a stackprof cpu window so the exact request count is known (44,707 req in 21.1 s). Conditions: arm64 Docker Desktop, one pinned core, 2 GB, ~2,100 rps with 20k open connections. Trust ranking: stackprof cpu (2,136 samples of ~1 ms CPU each, 1.48% miss) is the primary attribution; vernier wall mode under-sampled the running thread on the single core (898 busy samples = 1.7% while the process used ~12% CPU) and its stop/write of a 175 MB JSON stalled the server (p99 4.1 s, RSS 1.8 GB), so the wall profile is qualitative only and the bench line's pass:false is a profiling artifact; strace -c inflated per-request CPU to 65.5 us during its window, so use its counts, not its times. top_frames.frame: Extralite::Query#next (SQLite step: 92% from Store#feed, 7% Store#post, 1% Store#create)
IO::Event::Selector::URing#select (kernel socket I/O done inside io_uring_enter)
Store#begin_batch (total; 2.1% is Task#async spawning the commit fiber)

profile.findings:
Process CPU is 46-58 us/request at ~2,100 rps (stackprof window 45.8 us, vernier window 57.8 us incl. sampling overhead); the harness's cgroup figure (110.4 us/req in base.jsonl, 70.4 here) also contains kernel work outside the process context, which no Ruby profiler sees. Inside the process, by self CPU time (stackprof cpu, 2,136 samples):
1. SQLite inside extralite: ~45% (Query#next 36.6%, Database#execute 3.6%, Query#execute 2.9%, reset 1.3%, bind 0.4%) = roughly 20 us/req. 92% of Query#next is the Store#feed query (the SQLite-side JSON building for GET /feed), 7% GET /posts/:id; Database#execute splits COMMIT 60% / PASSIVE checkpoint 31% / BEGIN IMMEDIATE 9%; Query#execute is the like INSERT. This is C time in sqlite3; the Ruby side only controls how often and in what shape it is called.
2. Kernel socket I/O charged to io_uring_enter: ~20% (URing#select self 19.1% + Epoll.epoll_wait 1.0%). Every request costs at least three io_uring ops (1-byte wake read, read_nonblock through the scheduler, write) submitted in batches (~7 SQEs per io_uring_enter); zero read/recv/send syscalls appear in strace. Kernel time, not Ruby.
3. HTTP parsing/serialising/writing in Ruby: ~15-16% (IO#write 2.7% self / 4.2% total, header String#scan 2.2%, String#byteindex 1.4%, String.new 1.3%, drain+respond+service+work self 3.8%, URing io_read/io_write/transfer/resume 3.6%, Regexp#match? 0.6%, Integer#to_s/IO::Buffer#get_string <0.5%). HTTPServer#drain's own lines: scan block 2.5%, byteindex 0.7%, byteslices ~0.7%; respond: String.new 1.3%, `<<` 1.1%, write 4.3%.
4. Connection hand-off and scheduler: Thread::Queue push/pop plus the Integer#== inside Ruby's Queue#pop ~3%; Async bookkeeping (run_once! self, Timers#flush!, Fiber#initialize/Class#new for the per-batch commit task, Promise#wait, Mutex) ~4-5%. Group commit is per batch, not per request: begin_batch 5.1% total (2.1% of it spawning the commit fiber via Kernel#Async), commit 2.4%, checkpoint 1.1%.
5. GC 2.8% (sweeping 2.3%, marking 0.4%; 39 minor GCs per 60 s, ~1 us/req) and JWT auth 3.6% total (HMAC 0.8%, JSON parse of claims 0.9%, base64/byteslices the rest). YJIT is warm and steady (295 iseqs, 71 invalidations, 950 KB code).
Takeaways for later work: the only big Ruby-controllable levers are (a) the shape/cost of the feed statement and the per-batch BEGIN/COMMIT/checkpoint traffic (~45% total), (b) the number of io_uring submissions and parsing allocations per request (~35% kernel+parse), and (c) the small per-request fixed costs (Queue hand-off, scheduler, kwargs hash in String.new, header MatchData); everything else is already in the noise. Caveats: vernier wall mode is not trustworthy for CPU attribution on one pinned core here (1.7% busy samples vs ~12% CPU) and writing its profile stalls the server; strace -c distorts timings (65.5 us/req during its window) but not counts.
profile.syscalls: strace -c -f -p 1, 20 s inside the 20k-user hold (~42,400 requests in the window, derived from 44,707 req in the 21.1 s bracket): 59,499 syscalls total = 1.40 per request. pwrite64 24,222 (0.57/req; SQLite WAL frames + checkpoint page writes), io_uring_enter 17,806 (0.42/req, 80 EINTR/EAGAIN-type errors; carries all socket reads and writes, ~7 SQEs per call, no read/recv/send/write syscalls at all), epoll_pwait 7,252 (0.17/req, ~360/s = one FFI check of the parked-connection set per reactor pass, 62 us avg under ptrace), pread64 4,210 (0.10/req), madvise 2,478 (0.06/req, jemalloc purge), rt_sigreturn 2,723 (0.06/req, stackprof SIGPROF, profiler artifact), fsync 60 (3.0/s, 173 us avg, i.e. per checkpoint not per commit; synchronous=NORMAL WAL durability unchanged), ftruncate 40 (2/s), mprotect 326 and clock_gettime 330 (~16/s each), mremap 20, mmap/munmap/fstat/prctl <= 20. strace-measured syscall time 0.64 s per 20 s (epoll_pwait 71%, io_uring_enter 22%, pwrite64 4%) but ptrace inflated process CPU to 65.5 us/req in this window versus 45.8 unprofiled, so treat the time split as indicative only. Voluntary context switches ~2,250/s under strace (128k over 57 s).

ranked_variants.title: FEED without the aggregate ORDER BY (removes the temp b-tree sorter per /feed)
ranked_variants.spec:
File: submissions/ruby-async-cicloid/app.rb, class Store, constant FEED (currently lines 26-28). Replace with exactly:

FEED = "SELECT '{\"posts\":['||coalesce(group_concat(doc,','),'')||']}' " \
       "FROM (SELECT #{POST_JSON} AS doc FROM posts p JOIN users u ON u.id=p.user_id " \
       "ORDER BY p.created_at DESC,p.id DESC LIMIT 20)"

i.e. delete `ORDER BY created_at DESC,id DESC` inside group_concat and drop the now-unused `,p.created_at,p.id` projection of the subquery. Keep the subquery's ORDER BY ... LIMIT 20 verbatim (it is served as a CO-ROUTINE over posts_created_at_id_idx; group_concat consumes rows in co-routine order so bytes are unchanged). Nothing else changes: same `@feed = @db.prepare(FEED)` / prepare_splat, same `Store#feed` body (`@feed.reset.next; @feed.reset; @batch&.wait`).

Boot-time guard (add at the end of Store#initialize, after the prepares): keep the old text in a constant FEED_SORTED (the current string), run both once with `@db.query_single_value(FEED)` and `@db.query_single_value(FEED_SORTED)` (or prepare/next/reset so no statement is left mid-step) and `abort("feed plan drift")` if the two documents differ; also assert `@db.query("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN #{FEED}").none? { |r| r.values.join.include?("TEMP B-TREE") }`. This costs one feed at boot and turns any future plan change into a health failure instead of a reordered feed.

Edge cases: ties on created_at are still broken by `p.id DESC` inside the subquery; an empty posts table yields `{"posts":[]}` via coalesce as before. Do NOT touch sqlite_train.c here (toolchain rebuild not needed for this variant; v12 mirrors the text into the trainer).

Fallback if the reviewer refuses to rely on co-routine delivery order (same measured cost, 23.9 vs 23.2 us): make FEED the 20-row query `SELECT #{POST_JSON} FROM posts p JOIN users u ON u.id=p.user_id ORDER BY p.created_at DESC,p.id DESC LIMIT 20` (prepare_splat, `rows = @feed.reset.to_a; @feed.reset`) and build `'{"posts":[' + rows.join(',') + ']}'` in Ruby.

Verify: test/test.sh 42/42 (line ~121 checks the new post is posts[0]); byte-compare old vs new FEED on the seed DB before and after a few hundred mixed likes/creates (done by two proposers: identical 5102-byte documents); `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` shows no `USE TEMP B-TREE`; paired 20k bench (expect -8..-12 us per feed, feed = 46% of requests). Evidence: 31.9 -> 23.2 us per FEED in the PGO image, 64 -> 50 / 70 -> 53 / 39 -> 24 us in three other runs; opcodes 71 -> 59, VM steps 1048 -> 846.
ranked_variants.why_ranked_here: Largest single item by far: the FEED statement is 92% of Query#next which is 36.6% of the profile, and the sorter is ~25% of that statement. Byte-identical output, two independent measurements agree, one-constant change, no interaction with any other variant.

rules.problems:
No challenge-rule violation found; one API misconception that would make the variant fail test.sh as literally specified, plus one documented-behaviour dependency that the guard adequately covers.

1. API misconception (would break boot, 0/42): Extralite 3.1.3 (pinned in Gemfile.lock) has no `Database#query_single_value`. database.c registers only `query`, `query_splat`, `query_array`, `query_hash`, `query_single`, `query_single_array`, `query_single_splat`, `query_single_hash` (ext/extralite/database.c lines 1670-1677); the name survives only in a stale doc comment at lib/extralite.rb:252. Verified in the image: `db.respond_to?(:query_single_value) == false`. Store.new runs at server.rb:9 before warm-up/listen, so the guard would raise NoMethodError and the server would never become healthy.

2. Ordering dependency (not a rule violation, but worth stating): SQLite documents group_concat order as arbitrary without ORDER BY; the variant relies on the co-routine delivering rows in the subquery's ORDER BY order on the pinned SQLite 3540000 source built by install.sh. Empirically on the image's SQLite 3.54.0: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN for both texts is `CO-ROUTINE (subquery-2)` -> `SCAN p USING INDEX posts_created_at_id_idx` -> `SEARCH u ... rowid` -> correlated likes subquery; only OLD adds `USE TEMP B-TREE FOR group_concat(ORDER BY)`. Documents were byte-identical: seed 5102 B (golden feed.json check, test.sh:52), after 500 mixed likes/creates (compared every 100 ops), with 25 extra rows sharing the same created_at (id DESC tie-break inside the subquery), and `{"posts":[]}` on an empty schema. Flattening is impossible (subquery LIMIT + aggregate outer), and a MATERIALIZE plan would still preserve insertion order, so the only realistic drift path is a future SQLite change, which the boot comparison turns into an abort before listen. test.sh:119-123 (new post is posts[0], 20 rows) holds by construction. Note the EXPLAIN "TEMP B-TREE" assertion is a performance guard, not an ordering guard; the document comparison is the ordering guard and is only meaningful on a populated DB (always true for the challenge: fresh seed/feed.db).

3. Everything else is unchanged and compliant: SQLite only, schema/indexes untouched, no caching (the guard discards both boot documents; FEED_SORTED is SQL text, not data), prepared statements reused as before, WAL + synchronous=NORMAL and group-commit wait untouched, JWT verification untouched, no Gemfile/Gemfile.lock change so build-from-source and the gem layer are unaffected, no kernel or CPU tuning. sqlite_train.c still trains the old sorter path (PGO profile fidelity only; perf, not rules; v12 covers it).

Verification script: <scratchpad>/ref/verify.rb (run via `bundle exec ruby` in tdsc-cicloid:base against a scratch copy of seed/feed.db).
rules.spec_fixes:
1. Replace `@db.query_single_value(FEED)` and `@db.query_single_value(FEED_SORTED)` with `@db.query_single_splat(FEED)` and `@db.query_single_splat(FEED_SORTED)` (single-column row -> the String itself; the statement is fully stepped and finalized, nothing left mid-step). Alternative: `s = @db.prepare_splat(FEED_SORTED); doc = s.reset.next; s.reset; s.close`.

2. Keep `@db.query("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN #{FEED}")` as specified: it returns hash rows, and `r.values.join.include?("TEMP B-TREE")` matches the exact detail string SQLite 3.54 emits (`USE TEMP B-TREE FOR group_concat(ORDER BY)` on the old text, nothing on the new one). Use a distinct abort message for this check (e.g. `abort("feed plan uses a sorter")`) so a perf regression is distinguishable from an ordering regression.

3. Run the guard where the spec says (end of Store#initialize, after the prepares); that is before server.warm and listen (server.rb:9-22), so a drift aborts the process before it ever answers a request. Do not store either boot document in an ivar (keep the no-caching line clear).

4. Pin the dependency explicitly in the submission README's design notes: ordering relies on the co-routine delivery order of the pinned SQLite 3540000 build and is enforced at boot; comment in app.rb stays within the 3-line limit.

5. No change to Gemfile/Gemfile.lock, pragmas, sqlite_train.c or install.sh for this variant; the fallback (20-row query + Ruby join) remains acceptable if a reviewer rejects item 2, with identical bytes since the join uses ',' and the same wrapper literal.

tech.problems: 1) API misconception: `@db.query_single_value(...)` does not exist in extralite 3.1.3 (Database query methods are query, query_single, query_splat, query_single_splat, query_array, query_single_array, query_hash, query_single_hash, prepare*, execute, batch_*). `@db.query_single_splat(FEED)` returns the one-column String directly and is the drop-in (verified: String, 5102 bytes). The spec's parenthetical alternative (prepare/next/reset) also works. 2) Premise holds: SQLite 3.54 EQP for the current FEED shows `USE TEMP B-TREE FOR group_concat(ORDER BY)` and the new FEED shows none, same CO-ROUTINE over posts_created_at_id_idx; opcodes 71->59 (OpenEphemeral/IdxInsert gone). Output byte-identical on the seed DB (5102 B), after 400 mixed like/create batches including forced exact created_at ties, and on an empty posts table; Ruby-join fallback also identical. 3) Hot path confirmed from prof.cpu.methods.txt: Store#feed = 91.8% of Extralite::Query#next = 36.6% of CPU samples. 4) Cost: micro-bench in the image (10x5000, medians) current 33.0 us, new 23.5 us, Ruby-join fallback 24.6 us per feed. End to end, built as variant v01rev with the change + boot guard: test suite 42/42; paired 20k/60s bench base 49.3 us/req, 10.5% CPU, p95 2.04 ms vs v01rev 46.0 us/req, 9.8% CPU, p95 1.96 ms, 0 errors (-6.7% CPU/req; same-image pair noise ~0.3%; p99 9.0 vs 14.5 ms is within this harness's p99 noise, cf. aa20k 13.3 vs 73.5). Common path cannot get slower: strictly fewer VM steps, same plan, same bytes; the guard costs ~70 us once at boot and leaves no statement mid-step (query_single_splat/query are one-shot). 5) Ordering is deterministic per compiled bytecode, not by SQL contract; a prepared statement is only re-prepared on a schema-cookie change (none: fixed schema, no ANALYZE/VACUUM), so runtime drift is not a realistic risk. 6) Exact-bytes risk: none found; test line ~121 (new post is posts[0]) passes.
tech.spec_fixes: a) Replace `@db.query_single_value(FEED)` / `(FEED_SORTED)` with `@db.query_single_splat(FEED)` / `@db.query_single_splat(FEED_SORTED)`. b) Prefer fail-safe over abort: run the guard BEFORE `@feed = @db.prepare_splat(...)` and, on drift or a TEMP B-TREE line, `warn "feed plan drift: using sorted FEED"` and prepare FEED_SORTED instead; an abort turns a hypothetical planner difference on the droplet into a zero score, while the fallback only forfeits the ~4%. If abort is kept anyway, it is correct as written. Guard text that works verbatim in 3.1.3: `plan_ok = @db.query("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN #{FEED}").none? { |r| r.values.join.include?("TEMP B-TREE") }; same = @db.query_single_splat(FEED) == @db.query_single_splat(FEED_SORTED)`. c) Note for the write-up: expected end-to-end gain on this harness is ~3.3 us/req (-6.7% at 49 us/req); on the droplet's 111 us/req that is ~3-4%, consistent with expected_gain_pct 4. d) No change to server.rb warm-up is needed (GET /feed x50 already exercises the new statement); sqlite_train.c keeps training the sorter path until v12 mirrors the text, which is harmless. Review artifacts: variant dir local-bench/variants/v01rev, image tdsc-cicloid:v01rev, results local-bench/results/v01rev-pair-A.jsonl and v01rev-pair-B.jsonl.

ranked_variants.title: First read via read_nonblock into a per-worker String (no io_uring SQE, no IO::Buffer, no extra reactor pass)
ranked_variants.spec:
File: submissions/ruby-async-cicloid/http.rb. Verified in the image under the io_uring selector: `socket.read_nonblock(n, buf, exception: false)` is one direct recvfrom(2) with no fcntl and no io_uring_enter, and does not retain a per-IO rbuf on Ruby 4.0.7, whereas `Fiber.scheduler.io_read` is SQE + fiber transfer + enter + CQE + transfer back (scheduler version 3 has no optimistic read).

1. `work` (lines 144-154): replace `io_buffer = IO::Buffer.new(READ_SIZE)` with `inbuf = String.new(capacity: READ_SIZE)` and pass `inbuf` to `service`. Write the loop as `while true; begin; @waiting += 1; fd = @ready.pop; @waiting -= 1; service(fd, inbuf); rescue StandardError => error; Console.error(self, error); end; end` (while instead of `loop do` so break/return are jumps, not throws).

2. `service(fd, inbuf)` (lines 164-196): delete the `wait` flag and the whole `if wait ... Fiber.scheduler.io_read(socket, io_buffer, 1, 0) ... get_string ... else read_nonblock` expression. New inner read loop (both loops as `while true`):
   data = socket.read_nonblock(READ_SIZE, inbuf, exception: false)
   break if data == :wait_readable            # stale edge or nothing left: worker goes idle, no hold
   return disconnect(fd, socket) unless data  # nil = EOF
   buffer = if buffer then buffer << data      # buffer came from @partial or an earlier chunk: copies bytes
            elsif data.bytesize < READ_SIZE then data   # aliases inbuf: fine, consumed before the next read on this worker
            else data.dup                        # full chunk: must not alias inbuf because the next read overwrites it
            end
   break if data.bytesize < READ_SIZE
   After the loop keep `if buffer then rest = drain(socket, buffer) or return disconnect(fd, socket); @partial[fd] = rest.dup unless rest.empty? end` - the `.dup` is required because `rest` may be `buffer` itself (position 0) or a byteslice sharing inbuf, and inbuf is reused by this worker's next job; partial requests are rare so the copy is free. Keep `next if @state[fd] == AGAIN`, `@state[fd] = IDLE; return`, and `rescue IOError, SystemCallError -> disconnect`.

3. Update the comment block above `service`: a stale edge now returns :wait_readable immediately instead of parking the worker on a ring read, so pool growth for that case no longer happens (keep MAX_WORKERS as is). Keep `write(socket, data) = socket.write(data)` unchanged (ring writes; v03 is the separate write experiment).

Edge cases: the warm-up UNIXSocket pair in `warm` is blocking; read_nonblock sets O_NONBLOCK on it once (fcntl) - harmless. RDHUP-with-data behaves exactly as today (data read, short read breaks). Pipelined requests: drain already loops over the buffer. Requests larger than READ_SIZE: handled by the `data.dup` + `<<` path.

Verify: test/test.sh 42/42; hand tests: a request whose headers arrive in two writes 50 ms apart, two pipelined GETs in one write, a 9 KB POST body; strace of one keep-alive request shows recvfrom and no io_uring_enter for the read; paired 20k and 60k runs (expect ~1.3 us less I/O-path CPU per request plus one reactor pass fewer per batch). Prior evidence: io_read+get_string 1.72 us/op vs read_nonblock 0.39 us/op; end-to-end r1->r2 in a proposer's harness -4%.
ranked_variants.why_ranked_here: Attacks a verified structural cost (every first read is an SQE/CQE round trip plus two fiber transfers and an extra reactor pass per batch) with the smallest possible change; three lenses converged on the mechanism and my strace settled which call to use. Ranked above the write side because reads complete inline from the epoll-ready socket with no batching argument against it.

rules.problems: No rule violation found. The change is confined to the socket read path in http.rb; app.rb (JWT verified per request, WAL + synchronous=NORMAL, group commit waits for COMMIT), drain/respond (exact bytes, key order) and the build scripts are untouched, and a per-worker reusable read String is a buffer, not a cache: read_nonblock resets its length to the bytes just received, and every request's data still comes from SQLite. Evidence, all from the real image (Ruby 4.0.7, Async 2.46 on the io_uring selector): (1) built the spec's edit verbatim as local-bench/variants/v02-ref (image tdsc-cicloid:v02-ref); test/test.sh = passed=42 failed=0, so golden bytes still match. (2) Raw-socket hand tests all pass: headers in two writes 50 ms apart, two pipelined GETs in one write, a 9 KB POST body (full-chunk dup + '<<' path, answers 400 too long), a request of exactly 8192 bytes (full read then :wait_readable), 8192-byte request plus a pipelined one in the same write, POST head then body 50 ms later (rest == whole buffer -> dup), byte-by-byte request, client half-close (RDHUP with data), keep-alive rounds with think time, 50 concurrent pipelined triples and 50 concurrent fragmented requests, all in order and byte-identical to fresh-connection references. (3) 20k users / 60 s / ramp 20: 0 errors, p95 2.6 ms, p99 11.5 ms, 50.9 us/req, 10.9% CPU, 172 MB; a paired baseline run of tdsc-cicloid:base made right after gives 55.4 us/req, 11.8%, p99 16.0 ms (the 110.4 us line in results/base.jsonl is from an older harness state and is not comparable). (4) strace of one read_nonblock(8192, inbuf, exception: false) inside an Async fiber: exactly one recvfrom(fd, buf, 8192, MSG_DONTWAIT) with no fcntl and no io_uring_enter, and a prepended Async::Scheduler#io_read counter stays at 0, so the scheduler hook is not consulted; ObjectSpace.memsize_of(socket) stays 288 bytes before and after, so no per-IO rbuf is retained (the README's '4 KB IO buffer per read_nonblock' side-finding is wrong on this Ruby). (5) read_nonblock returns inbuf itself (equal? true, ASCII-8BIT), returns nil and empties inbuf at EOF, :wait_readable when empty. Misconceptions in the spec's reasoning, none affecting correctness: 'data.dup' and an end-of-buffer byteslice do not copy bytes on CRuby; they share the heap buffer with a new frozen root, and the next read_nonblock into inbuf triggers rb_str_modify -> str_make_independent (malloc + memcpy of inbuf's current length, then an expand back to READ_SIZE). The .dup calls are still required (rest may literally be inbuf, and 'buffer << data' with buffer.equal?(inbuf) would self-append), but the copy cost lands on the next read of that worker, on every full chunk and on every request whose body (>16 bytes) ends the buffer, i.e. POST /posts. Verified empirically that body slices and dups stay intact across the next read. The 'read_nonblock sets O_NONBLOCK once via fcntl on the warm-up pair' remark is moot: on 4.0.7 socket read_nonblock uses recvfrom(MSG_DONTWAIT) and never calls fcntl. ET lost-wakeup analysis: a stale edge now goes IDLE instead of parking; every byte arriving after the worker's last read raises a new edge that becomes AGAIN (if BUSY) or a push (if IDLE), so no wakeup is lost; confirmed by the think-time load run with 0 errors.

ranked_variants.title: Response write via write_nonblock (direct sendto), io_uring write only for the partial/EAGAIN remainder
ranked_variants.spec:
File: submissions/ruby-async-cicloid/http.rb, method `write` (lines 292-294). Replace the body with:

  def write(socket, data)
    written = socket.write_nonblock(data, exception: false)
    return if written == data.bytesize
    written = 0 if written == :wait_writable
    socket.write(data.byteslice(written, data.bytesize - written)) # ring path handles POLLOUT + the rest
  end

Verified in the image: write_nonblock is one direct sendto(2) with no fcntl and no io_uring_enter; socket.write and syswrite both go through the ring (SQE, fiber transfer, enter, CQE, transfer back, plus an IO::Buffer wrapper allocation in rb_io_write). Responses are 60 B-5 KB and the send buffer is empty in this workload, so the fast path completes inline essentially always.

Edge cases: EPIPE/ECONNRESET raise SystemCallError exactly as socket.write did and are caught by service's rescue -> disconnect; a partial write (large /feed under backpressure) falls back to the existing ring write so bytes are unchanged; the warm-up UNIXSocket pair is blocking and drained after each request, write_nonblock just flips it to O_NONBLOCK once. Update the comment above `write` (it currently says writes are batched through io_uring).

Risk to measure, not argue: README reports io_uring batching of reads+writes cut CPU 46%->40% at 40k on the target; local micro (16 concurrent writers so SQEs batch per enter) still favours write_nonblock 0.77 vs 1.71 us/op, but one sendto per response replaces one amortised SQE. So this variant MUST be benchmarked paired at 20k AND 60k (or 80k if the slot allows) and only adopted if both are flat-or-better. Verify: test/test.sh 42/42; strace shows sendto per response and io_uring_enter count per request drops; compare us_per_req and p99.
ranked_variants.why_ranked_here: Same mechanism class as v02 but kept separate because the README's io_uring-batching claim means the write side could regress at saturation; a 3-line change whose A/B settles a standing design question.

rules.problems:
No rule violation found. Checked against README "Rules" 2-7, 10-11 and SPEC.md, and verified empirically on the exact patch (built as local-bench/variants/v03-ref -> image tdsc-cicloid:v03-ref; the only diff vs the submission is the `write` method in http.rb).

Evidence:
- test/test.sh via `bench.sh tdsc-cicloid:v03-ref v03-ref --test`: passed=42 failed=0 (golden feed/post bytes, content-type, all error bodies, create/like/read-back).
- strace of the patched server (tdsc-cicloid:strace with the patched http.rb mounted over /app/http.rb) under live requests: 8 responses -> exactly 8 `sendto(fd, "HTTP/1.1 ...", n, MSG_DONTWAIT, NULL, 0) = n`, every one complete (incl. the 5175-byte /feed, a pipelined pair, the `connection: close` reply and an HTTP/1.0 reply); zero fcntl on the client sockets; no ring write SQEs for responses. In the same trace `socket.write` (control test) produced no direct syscall and went through io_uring_enter, so the claim "write_nonblock = one direct sendto, socket.write = ring" is correct. Peer-reset socket: write_nonblock raised Errno::ECONNRESET (SystemCallError), which service's `rescue IOError, SystemCallError` turns into disconnect, as before. Ruby's SIGPIPE handler is a no-op, so EPIPE cannot kill the process.
- Durability (rule 6) is untouched: a 201 is written only after `batch.wait` returns, which resolves only after `@db.execute("COMMIT")` returns (app.rb 76-94, 127-135); strace shows the WAL frame pwrite64s preceding each `sendto(... "HTTP/1.1 201 ...")`. Pragmas, group commit, JWT verification, SQLite-only, build-from-source and no-kernel-tuning are unaffected (one Ruby method changed, no new gems/C).
- Ordering/exact bytes: the response string is built identically in `respond`; the fallback `socket.write(data.byteslice(written, rest))` goes through io-event's io_write loop, which handles EAGAIN via io_wait and writes until all bytes are out, so pipelined responses stay in order and byte-identical.

Minor misconceptions in the spec text (not violations):
1. "write_nonblock just flips it to O_NONBLOCK once" is wrong on Linux: Ruby's BasicSocket#write_nonblock is `__write_nonblock` -> send(2) with MSG_DONTWAIT (/opt/ruby/lib/ruby/4.0.0/socket.rb lines 462-469 in the image). It never touches the fd flags (no fcntl observed). Harmless for the warm-up pair: a would-block there falls to `socket.write`, which with no scheduler running yet simply blocks.
2. Behavioural note to keep in mind when reading the paired bench: after a direct send the worker fiber no longer yields, it goes straight to `@ready.pop`, which returns without yielding while the queue is non-empty; each `service` still yields at its first scheduler `io_read`, so dispatch and the commit task still run every pass. Not a correctness or rules issue.
3. If adopted, the submission README would contradict the code (it says reads AND writes are batched through io_uring and that this cut CPU 46%->40%); README accuracy is part of the submission even though it is not a scored rule.

2. Keep the fallback exactly as `socket.write(data.byteslice(written, data.bytesize - written))` (scheduler io_write path), not syswrite/another write_nonblock loop: io-event's loop already handles EAGAIN via io_wait and preserves per-connection response order.

Add a README task to the variant: update the "io_uring for socket reads and writes" bullet (reads batched via io_uring; each response is one direct non-blocking send, with the ring used only for a partial/would-block remainder) and the "writes each response with one `write`" wording in the first bullet and the class comment at http.rb line 6-8; either re-measure or attribute the 46%->40% figure to the previous read+write batching.

Premise verified in the image; nothing refutes it, but two claims need correcting and the saturation A/B is unresolved.
