ranked_variants.title: Group commit as a deferred synchronous flush: no Task/Fiber/Promise per batch, no reader waits, LIKE as VALUES upsert
ranked_variants.spec:
File: submissions/ruby-async-cicloid/app.rb, class Store (write path lines 60-137). Design: writers only ENQUEUE their operation and yield once; the first writer that resumes runs every pending operation inside one BEGIN IMMEDIATE ... COMMIT synchronously (no fiber switch inside), so a transaction is never open across a fiber switch, readers can never observe uncommitted rows and therefore never need to wait, and each writer responds only after the COMMIT that contained its statement.

1. Remove `require "async/promise"`, `@batch`, `@checkpoint_due`, `begin_batch`, `commit`. In `initialize` add `@pending = []` and prepared transaction statements `@begin = @db.prepare("BEGIN IMMEDIATE"); @commit = @db.prepare("COMMIT"); @rollback = @db.prepare("ROLLBACK")` (call `.execute` on them; a proposer measured the pair 0.57 -> 0.27 us). Change `LIKE` to `"INSERT INTO likes(user_id,post_id) VALUES(?1,?2) ON CONFLICT(user_id,post_id) DO NOTHING"`; the `@exists` statement can be deleted (PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON stays: it is what turns a missing post into an error).

2. `feed` and `post`: delete the `@batch&.wait` line (keep the reset-immediately pattern). `checkpoint` (called every second from server.rb): simply `checkpoint!` - no batch can be open when the timer task runs.

3. Writers:
  def create(user_id, username, body) = enqueue([:create, user_id, body, username])
  def like(user_id, post_id) = enqueue([:like, user_id, post_id])
  def enqueue(op)
    slot = []                      # [result] or [nil, error]; frozen once its flush finished
    @pending << [op, slot]
    Fiber.scheduler&.yield         # every request ready in this reactor pass enqueues before anyone flushes (warm-up has no scheduler)
    flush unless slot.frozen?      # first writer back from the yield flushes for all; later ones find their slot done
    raise slot[1] if slot[1]
    slot[0]
  end
  def flush
    ops = @pending; @pending = []
    return if ops.empty?
    @begin.execute
    ops.each do |op, slot|
      slot[0] = run_op(op)
    rescue Extralite::Error => error   # statement failure: only this request fails, SQLite rolled back just that statement
      slot[1] = error
    end
    begin
      @commit.execute
    rescue Extralite::Error => error   # COMMIT failure: every op of this flush fails
      @rollback.execute if @db.transaction_active?
      ops.each { |_, slot| slot[0] = nil; slot[1] ||= error }
    end
    ops.each { |_, slot| slot.freeze }
  end
  def run_op(op)
    case op[0]
    when :create then document = @create.bind(op[1], op[2], op[3]).next; @create.reset; document
    when :like
      begin
        @like.execute(op[1], op[2]) == 1 ? :liked : :already_liked
      rescue Extralite::Error => error
        raise unless error.message.start_with?("FOREIGN KEY constraint failed")  # likes.post_id REFERENCES posts(id)
        :missing
      end
    end
  end
  flush must contain no fiber switch: Extralite runs with gvl_release_threshold=-1 and the statements are synchronous, so none exists; do not add logging or sleeps inside it.

4. App#like / App#create keep their 201/200/404 mapping (`:missing` -> 404). Verify once in the image that a like on a missing id raises Extralite::Error with message starting "FOREIGN KEY constraint failed" (SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_FOREIGNKEY); if this extralite exposes the sqlite error code, match on code 787 instead of the text. An FK failure aborts only the statement, the batch transaction stays open and committable (a proposer verified 5k rescued FK errors inside one BEGIN IMMEDIATE then COMMIT).

Semantics preserved: each write response is sent only after its COMMIT (rule 6, WAL + synchronous=NORMAL unchanged); the batch is still 'everything ready in this pass' because enqueue yields exactly like today's `task.yield`; LIKE's duplicate check and CREATE's RETURNING run one pass later, invisible to clients. No reader ever sees a row that could fail to commit (the property the README documents is kept by construction, which is why reads-skip-batch-wait is subsumed, not adopted). Remove the README paragraph about reads waiting for the batch and describe the flush.

Verify: test/test.sh 42/42; burst test: 50 concurrent likes on one post (exactly one :liked), duplicate likes, like of a missing post (404), create + immediate feed; force a COMMIT failure (temporarily raise in flush after @begin) and check all writers of that flush get 500 and the next flush works; `strace -c` shows no madvise per batch and fewer BEGIN/COMMIT per second at a POST burst; paired 20k bench and, since per-batch costs are fixed while batches grow with load, a 60k pair.
ranked_variants.why_ranked_here: Five proposals from three lenses attack the same verified overhead (Async::Task + Fiber + Promise per batch, Promise#wait YJIT fallback, Ruby-implemented ConditionVariable waits for every reader that lands in a write pass, ~4-5% of the profile). The deferred-flush shape is the simplest of them, removes reader waits without weakening consistency, and absorbs the LIKE upsert (both like proposals measured -3 us per like) because it rewrites Store#like anyway.

rules.problems:
No rule violation found. Verified in tdsc-cicloid:base against a fresh copy of seed/feed.db (scripts: <scratchpad>/ref/store_check.rb and .../ref/fiber_check.rb): SQLite 3.54.0, PRAGMA foreign_keys=1, no OMIT_FOREIGN_KEY in compile_options; inside a prepared BEGIN IMMEDIATE a like on post 999999999 raises Extralite::Error with message exactly "FOREIGN KEY constraint failed" and Database#errcode == 787 (extended codes are on); transaction_active? stays true; the next like.execute(1,1) inserts with fresh bindings (changes=1, repeat 0) because extralite's query_bind calls sqlite3_reset before binding; CREATE ... RETURNING via bind(...).next; reset works in the batch; COMMIT succeeds after errored statements; 5000 rescued FK errors then COMMIT ok; ROLLBACK path and the following flush ok; prepared BEGIN/COMMIT re-execute fine; PASSIVE checkpoint ok afterwards. Async 2.46.0: Async::Scheduler#yield exists (Fiber.scheduler is an Async::Reactor inside worker tasks; Fiber.scheduler&.yield is nil-safe in warm-up, which issues no writes). The enqueue/flush simulation returned every writer its own result, a failing op failed alone, and the no-scheduler path flushed inline. test/test.sh mapping: like(first) changes=1 -> 201; like(repeat) 0 -> 200; like missing post FK -> 404; POST /posts/1/like after the FK error binds (1,1) correctly so "counted at once" passes; response bytes for feed/post/create are unchanged SQL. Durability (rule 6) holds by construction: a writer returns from enqueue only after the synchronous flush that contained its statement committed, or with its slot's error. No caching (rule 5): slots hold one request's result until that writer reads it.

Risks that are not violations but should be fixed: (1) Wrong assumption: the FK rescue cannot tell likes.post_id from likes.user_id failures; both produce the identical Extralite::Error "FOREIGN KEY constraint failed" / errcode 787 (observed). A like by a user id absent from users on an existing post would answer 404 "post not found" where SPEC.md's table reserves 404 for a missing post and sends everything else to 500 (current code answers 500). Untested path (test uses user 1; load uses seeded users 1-20000), but a spec deviation. (2) flush is not exception-safe: a non-Extralite StandardError escaping run_op or the COMMIT block leaves the transaction open across fiber switches (readers would then see uncommitted rows, every later BEGIN IMMEDIATE fails with "cannot start a transaction within a transaction", the 1 s checkpoint fails) and leaves the other writers' slots unfrozen: they find @pending empty, return slot[0]=nil, App#create yields [201, nil] and respond raises NoMethodError, which work's rescue swallows, leaving that connection BUSY forever. Rare in practice (realistic errors are all Extralite::Error) but cheap to close. (3) Batching granularity: in the simulation task.async-spawned writers batched in pairs because fibers resumed during a ready-queue flush land in the next flush; in the server, workers resumed from io completions yield into the same flush, so the batch should still be "everything enqueued before the first writer resumes", but do not assume parity with the old committer task: measure BEGIN/COMMIT per second as the spec already plans.
rules.spec_fixes: 1. Keep @exists for the cold FK path only: in run_op(:like), on an Extralite::Error whose message starts with "FOREIGN KEY constraint failed" (or @db.errcode == 787, read inside the rescue before any other statement runs on the connection; both are valid, pick one), run `exists = @exists.bind(op[2]).next; @exists.reset; exists ? raise : :missing`. That restores the current 404-only-when-the-post-is-missing / 500-otherwise behaviour at zero cost on the hot path (the check runs only when the insert failed), and keeps the README sentence "a post-existence check runs only when nothing was inserted" true. 2. Make flush exception-safe: rescue StandardError (not only Extralite::Error) per op; wrap begin..ops..commit in begin/rescue StandardError/ensure so that on any escape the code does `@rollback.execute if @db.transaction_active?` (itself inside a rescue), sets slot[0]=nil and slot[1]||=error on every slot, and the ensure freezes every slot. Invariant to state in the spec: flush never returns or raises with the transaction active or with an unfrozen slot. 3. Amend the errcode clause: Extralite::Database#errcode exists and returns the extended code (787 observed for this failure), so "match on code 787" is possible; the message match is equally exact. 4. README: besides removing the reads-wait sentence, rewrite the "Group commit" bullet (first writer back from its yield runs the whole batch synchronously; no transaction is open across a fiber switch) and the "Likes in one statement" bullet (VALUES upsert; the FK on likes.post_id signals a missing post; existence check only on that path), since the README must describe the optimizations actually in the code. 5. Keep the spec's "no logging or sleeps inside flush" as a hard requirement: Console.error/warn write to stderr through the fiber scheduler and can switch fibers, which would break the no-open-transaction-across-switches property. 6. Add to the verify list: like on an existing post with a token whose sub is not a seeded user id -> 500 (not 404); and after a 404 like, a like on a different existing post inserts the new pair (guards the bind-reset assumption).

tech.problems:
Premise holds; nothing refutes it. Verified in tdsc-cicloid:base (Ruby 4.0.7 YJIT, async 2.46.0, io-event 1.22.1, extralite 3.1.3, SQLite 3.54.0):
- Async::Scheduler#yield exists (scheduler.rb:199, `@selector.yield`) and Task#yield is literally `Fiber.scheduler.yield` (task.rb:158). io-event's yield = push self to the ready queue + transfer to the loop (selector.h:183); URing#select runs ready_flush BEFORE processing completions (uring.c:1671-1673) and a flush stops at a placeholder, so fibers pushed during a flush run in the next one: the batching window ("everything ready in this pass") is identical to today's committer. Micro-bench confirms flush counts are identical old vs new in every config (2409/2409, 1957/1957, 800/800). Fiber.scheduler is nil outside Async (warm-up safe; warm-up never reaches Store writers anyway).
- extralite: `db.prepare("BEGIN IMMEDIATE").execute` works; FK failure on a missing post raises base Extralite::Error (not SQLError) with message exactly "FOREIGN KEY constraint failed"; extended result codes are enabled and `Database#errcode` returns 787 inside the rescue (there is no code accessor on the exception; errcode goes stale, e.g. 101, after any later successful call, and `transaction_active?` is fine to call after reading it). Transaction stays active through 5,000 rescued FK errors and then COMMITs; `@create.bind(...).next` works without a leading reset (Query#bind does sqlite3_reset+clear_bindings itself); VALUES upsert `execute` returns 1 then 0.
- Hot path: the existing 20k profile (local-bench/results/prof.cpu.summary.txt) attributes Async::Task#async 2.1%, Promise#wait 1.5%, Fiber#initialize/Task#finish!/Promise#initialize ~0.8% => ~4% total, matching the spec's claim. Store micro-bench (worker pool + Thread::Queue, YJIT threshold 5, OLD then NEW in the same container, 2 pairs per config): writes-only batch=1: 35.9/34.6 -> 20.8/20.4 us per write; batch=16: 16.9/16.7 -> 13.3/11.8; 8% writes batch=1: 24.3/24.2 -> 23.2/21.2 us/job; 8% writes batch=8: 22.9/23.5 -> 20.3/19.1. NEW was never slower in 8 pairs. strace -c on 8,000 single-write batches: madvise 10,011 -> 10, minor faults 24,653 -> 588 (committer fiber stack released and re-faulted per batch), pwrite64 identical 71,781 (same WAL traffic).
- Expected size: ~14 us saved per single-write batch and ~4 us per write in 16-write batches; at 7.8% writes that is ~1 us/req at 20k (~1-1.5% of 65-110 us/req) and less at 60k where batches are larger. That is below this harness's run-to-run noise (base 20k runs span 55.7-110.4 us/req), so a paired bench will not resolve it; the micro-bench and strace deltas are the evidence.
Minor issues (not blockers): (1) flush is not exception-safe for a BEGIN failure or a non-Extralite exception inside run_op: the exception escapes from the first writer, the other slots stay unfrozen, those writers call flush on an empty @pending and return nil (App#create then hands nil to respond -> NoMethodError, connection left BUSY forever), and the transaction stays open so every later BEGIN raises "cannot start a transaction within a transaction" and reads would see uncommitted rows. (2) Behaviour change: a like on an existing post by a user id absent from users now yields FK -> :missing -> 404 (today 500); both FKs produce the same message/code. Untested by test.sh (tokens are seeded users) and off-spec either way. (3) The verification expectation "fewer BEGIN/COMMIT per second" is wrong: transaction count is unchanged by construction; the observable syscall difference is madvise/page faults, not pwrite64. (4) sqlite_train.c still trains the PGO build on the old INSERT...SELECT WHERE EXISTS statement plus the EXISTS probe; harmless but the profile no longer matches the hot statement.
tech.spec_fixes:
1. FK detection: match on `@db.errcode == 787` read as the first thing inside the rescue (Database#errcode, extended codes are on), or keep the exact message match "FOREIGN KEY constraint failed"; both verified. Do not read errcode after any other extralite call.
2. Make flush exception-safe. Rescue StandardError (not only Extralite::Error) per op, and wrap the BEGIN: if `@begin.execute` raises, mark every slot `[nil, error]`, freeze them and return. After the commit/rollback block, `@rollback.execute if @db.transaction_active?` as a final guard so no transaction ever survives a flush. In enqueue, after `flush unless slot.frozen?`, raise (e.g. RuntimeError "write lost") if the slot is still unfrozen instead of returning nil, so App returns 500 rather than crashing respond with a nil document.
3. Optional, zero hot-path cost: keep `@exists` and use it only in the FK rescue (`@exists.reset.bind(post_id).next ? raise : :missing`) to preserve today's 404-vs-500 split for a missing user; otherwise document that a missing user on a like now maps to 404.
4. Verification section: expect the SAME number of BEGIN/COMMIT (and pwrite64) per second as today under a POST burst; expect madvise to drop to ~0 per batch and minor faults per write to fall (measured 10,011->10 madvise and 24,653->588 minflt per 8,000 batches). Judge the CPU gain by the micro-bench numbers above; the 20k/60k pairs will be within harness noise (base 20k runs vary 55-110 us/req), so do not treat a flat pair as a refutation.
5. Expected gain: revise to ~1% at 20k (14 us per single-write batch x 7.8% writes) and ~0.5% at 60k where batches are larger; readers no longer block on an open batch, which removes one fiber block/unblock for the ~25% of reads that land after a write in the same pass.
6. Optional follow-up (separate variant, rebuilds the toolchain layer): update sqlite_train.c's LIKE string to the VALUES form and drop the EXISTS probe so SQLite's PGO profile matches the new statement.

ranked_variants.title: Parser/response/app micro trims: byteindex header walker, interpolated response, TRIM fast path, lean JWT verify, bind-reset trim
ranked_variants.spec:
Files: submissions/ruby-async-cicloid/http.rb (drain, respond) and app.rb (App#create, App#authenticate, Store#post). Five independent edits; land them in this order and keep test/test.sh at 42/42 after each.

(a) http.rb `respond` (lines 284-289): replace the String.new(capacity:)+<< assembly with one interpolation:
  def respond(socket, heads, status, document)
    write(socket, "#{heads[status] || heads[500]}#{document.bytesize}\r\n\r\n#{document}")
  end
Heads are frozen ASCII literals, document is UTF-8 JSON, bytes are identical. (String.new with a keyword allocates 2 Hashes via rb_scan_args; measured 5 objects/0.93 us -> 2 objects/0.54 us per response.) END_HEAD stays for the parser.

(b) http.rb `drain` header block (lines 239-257): replace `buffer.byteslice(line_end, head_end - line_end).scan(HEADER) do ... end` with a byte walker over the header lines. Add constants `CRLF = "\r\n"`, `COLON = ":"`, `CONTENT_LENGTH = "content-length"`, `TRANSFER_ENCODING = "transfer-encoding"`, `CONNECTION = "connection"`, `AUTHORIZATION = "authorization"`. Algorithm (pos = line_end + 2; while pos < head_end): eol = buffer.byteindex(CRLF, pos); colon = buffer.byteindex(COLON, pos); if colon && colon < eol: name_end = colon, step back over trailing SP/HT (bytes 32/9) to get name_len; only when name_len is 14, 17, 10 or 13 do: v0 = colon+1 skipping SP/HT, v1 = eol stepping back over SP/HT, value = buffer.byteslice(v0, v1 - v0), name = buffer.byteslice(pos, name_len); then the existing case: 14 -> `return reject(socket, 400) unless DIGITS.match?(value); length = value.to_i` if name.casecmp?(CONTENT_LENGTH); 17 -> `return reject(socket, 411)` if name.casecmp?(TRANSFER_ENCODING); 10 -> existing CLOSE_TOKEN / KEEP_ALIVE_TOKEN logic if name.casecmp?(CONNECTION); 13 -> `authorization = value` if name.casecmp?(AUTHORIZATION). Lines without a colon are skipped (as the regex did). pos = eol + 2. Remove HEADER and TRAILING_BLANKS if unused. This is byte-equivalent to the regex for the four names (case-insensitive name at line start, optional blanks before the colon and around the value, trailing blanks trimmed) and keeps the same 400/411/413 outcomes. Measured: POST head with a 200-byte token 6.0 us/18 objects -> 1.09 us/9 objects; GET /feed head 0.385 -> 0.198 us.

(c) app.rb App#create: replace `body = body.gsub(TRIM, "")` with `first = body.getbyte(0); last = body.getbyte(-1); body = body.gsub(TRIM, "") unless first && first.between?(0x21, 0x7E) && last.between?(0x21, 0x7E)`. Every JS-whitespace character is ASCII 0x09-0x0D/0x20 or a multibyte sequence whose first byte >= 0xC2 and last byte is 0x80-0xBF, so printable ASCII at both ends proves nothing to trim; empty body falls through to gsub then the existing empty check. Rest of create unchanged.

(d) app.rb Store#post: `document = @post.bind(id).next; @post.reset` (drop the leading `.reset`: extralite's Query#bind sets should_reset and next resets before stepping; the trailing reset MUST stay so no read transaction is held open across the checkpoint). Leave `feed` as is.

(e) app.rb App#authenticate (lines 274-314), behaviour-preserving rewrite: (1) in module Sodium attach directly `crypto_auth_hmacsha256_statebytes [] -> :size_t`, `crypto_auth_hmacsha256_init [:pointer,:pointer,:size_t] -> :int`, `crypto_auth_hmacsha256_update [:pointer,:pointer,:ulong_long] -> :int`, `crypto_auth_hmacsha256_final [:pointer,:pointer] -> :int`, and `crypto_verify_32 [:pointer,:pointer] -> :int`; (2) in App#initialize build the keyed state once: `size = Sodium.crypto_auth_hmacsha256_statebytes; tmpl = FFI::MemoryPointer.new(size); Sodium.crypto_auth_hmacsha256_init(tmpl, @key, @key.bytesize); @hmac_template = tmpl.get_bytes(0, size); @hmac_state = FFI::MemoryPointer.new(size); @mac = FFI::MemoryPointer.new(32)`; (3) authenticate: `raise Halt.new(401, MISSING_TOKEN) unless header&.start_with?("Bearer ")`; find `first = header.index(".", 7)`, `last = header.rindex(".")`; reject (401 INVALID_TOKEN) unless first && first != last && header.bytesize - last - 1 == 43; `signing = header.byteslice(7, last - 7)`; `@hmac_state.put_bytes(0, @hmac_template); update(signing); final(@mac)`; decode the signature segment strictly (base64url -> base64 via `tr("-_", "+/")`, pad by length mod 4: 0 none, 2 "==", 3 "=", 1 -> reject; `unpack1("m0")` raising ArgumentError -> 401) and compare with `crypto_verify_32`; then decode header/payload segments the same strict way, keep every existing check (alg header must equal HS256_HEADER bytes, `exp` numeric and > now using `Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_REALTIME)`, `sub` numeric). Drop the BASE64URL regex pre-checks only where `m0` strictness already rejects the same inputs; keep the fixed 43-char signature check. The template holds the keyed ipad/opad state (key material, not a per-request cache; no token memoization). Measured 5,110 ns/22 objects -> ~3,960 ns/14 objects per verify.

Verify after each edit: test/test.sh 42/42 (401 cases, trimming cases, 500/501-char body cases, Connection: close handling); for (e) also hand-built tokens with wrong alg, expired exp, non-numeric sub, signature of 42/44 chars, payload length 1 mod 4. Paired 20k bench once with all five.
ranked_variants.why_ranked_here: Six high-confidence, byte-identical trims that each remove measured allocations or regex work in the ~15% Ruby HTTP/app slice (header scan 2.2%, String.new 1.3%, JWT 3.6%); bundled because they touch disjoint code and are too small to A/B alone against the harness noise. Below v04 only because the aggregate is smaller than a structural change.

rules.problems:
No inherent rule violation: SQLite/schema/pragmas/group-commit untouched, documents still built by SQLite or frozen constants (bytes and key order unchanged), no new gems or C extensions (FFI attach only), no caching across requests (the HMAC template is the keyed ipad/opad state derived from JWT_SECRET alone, equivalent to key material; every token's MAC is still computed and compared). Verified in the base image: extralite 3.1.3 Query#bind already calls sqlite3_reset and sets should_reset, and #next resets before stepping, so (d) is byte-identical; copying the 208-byte crypto_auth_hmacsha256_state reproduces crypto_auth_hmacsha256's MAC; JSON 3.1.0 raises on lone surrogates so (c) never sees invalid UTF-8; every multibyte JS-whitespace char in SPACE starts >= 0xC2 and ends 0x80-0xBF.

Three spec defects that could silently produce a non-compliant build:
1. (e) says only "compare with crypto_verify_32". A raw attach_function returns Integer 0 (match) or -1 (mismatch); -1 is truthy in Ruby, so `raise ... unless Sodium.crypto_verify_32(...)` NEVER rejects. Critically, test/test.sh would still pass 42/42: its "bad signature" case uses a 55-char signature, rejected by the bytesize==43 check before any HMAC runs, and every other test token is validly signed. The suite never exercises a well-formed wrong signature, so this would ship a server that accepts any token (rule 5 violation) undetected. The spec's own hand-test list (42/44-char signatures) also misses this case.
2. (e) claims the BASE64URL pre-check can be dropped "where m0 strictness already rejects the same inputs". False for the signature: `("A"*42+"=")` is 43 chars, padded to 44, and unpack1("m0") accepts it, yielding 31 bytes; crypto_verify_32 then reads 1 byte past the string (not a forgery path, since 32 bytes must still match, but an out-of-bounds read the old regex prevented). m0 also accepts '+' and '/' and embedded padding, so header/payload segments in standard-base64 or padded form become accepted where they were 401 before (lenient, untested, not a rule breach, but not "behaviour-preserving" as claimed).
3. (b) all-blank values ("Content-Length:   \r\n") give v1 < v0 so byteslice returns nil; outcomes coincidentally match (Regexp#match?(nil) is false, nil&.start_with? -> 401 missing token) but the back-steps are unbounded. Also a bare CR or LF inside a header line now runs the value to the CRLF where the regex stopped at the CR/LF; stricter (400/401 instead of truncation), acceptable.
rules.spec_fixes:
(e)-1 MANDATORY: write the compare as `raise Halt.new(401, INVALID_TOKEN) unless Sodium.crypto_verify_32(@mac, decoded).zero?` (same for any other raw attach: treat the Integer return explicitly). Keep `sodium_function :hmac_sha256` in module Sodium because server.rb's warm-up calls it. Add to the hand tests a VALID token with one character of its 43-char signature flipped (and the decoded-length case below) expecting 401 "invalid or expired token"; test/test.sh cannot catch a broken compare.
(e)-2 MANDATORY: keep `BASE64URL.match?(signature)` on the 43-char signature (or, at minimum, `raise 401 unless decoded.bytesize == 32` before crypto_verify_32) so no '=' / '+' / '/' reaches the decoder and crypto_verify_32 always reads exactly 32 bytes. For header/payload segments either keep the BASE64URL check (one match? on ~100 bytes is cheap) or accept and document the leniency; "behaviour-preserving" is only true with the checks kept.
(e)-3 Make explicit that "keep every existing check" includes: the fallback `parse_segment(head)` with `fields["alg"] == "HS256"` when head != HS256_HEADER (do not turn it into a byte-equality-only test; SPEC says accept HS256, not one serialization), the `nbf` check, `username.is_a?(String)` -> 401 INVALID_PAYLOAD, and `sub` positive and <= MAX_ID. Use byteindex/byterindex for the dot search so correctness does not depend on the header value being BINARY.
(b) Bound both back-steps: `name_end -= 1 while name_end > pos && blank(buffer.getbyte(name_end - 1))` and `v1 -= 1 while v1 > v0 && blank(buffer.getbyte(v1 - 1))`, so byteslice lengths are never negative and an empty value is "" (as the regex produced), not nil. Note in the README that a bare CR/LF inside a header line is now rejected rather than truncated.
(a),(c),(d): no amendment needed; keep the trailing `@post.reset` as stated.

tech.problems:
1. (e) is NOT behaviour-preserving as written. `unpack1("m0")` is strict about the alphabet [A-Za-z0-9+/=] and padding, but after `tr("-_", "+/")` it accepts inputs the dropped BASE64URL pre-check rejected. Demonstrated with real tokens (scratchpad probe_b64b.rb): a signature in the standard base64 alphabet ("/" instead of "_") -> old 401, new accepted; a payload segment carrying "=" padding with length % 4 == 0 -> old 401, new accepted (MAC verifies because it is over the raw segment). The 43-char signature ending in "=" happens to still give 401, but only because strict64 yields 31 bytes and crypto_verify_32 reads the String's NUL terminator as byte 32 (a 1-byte over-read). The spec's own condition "drop the regex only where m0 already rejects the same inputs" is therefore not met for "+", "/" and "=".

2. (b) walker has a pathological regression the regex did not have: `buffer.byteindex(COLON, pos)` is unbounded, so each colon-less header line re-scans the whole remaining buffer (body + pipelined data). Measured on a 16 KB head of colon-less lines followed by a 1 MB colon-free body already in the buffer: regex 0.2-0.4 ms vs spec walker 30-33 ms per drain, and drain re-parses the head on every read batch while a body is arriving (~128 batches for 1 MB), i.e. seconds of CPU for one malicious request. Not on the common path, but a DoS amplification versus the baseline. Memoizing the colon as the spec suggests does NOT fix it unless a miss is memoized too (with `nil` memoization it stayed at 30 ms).

3. (b) "byte-equivalent to the regex" is false for a bare CR or LF inside a field value: "Authorization: Bearer x\rjunk\r\n" -> regex value "Bearer x", walker "Bearer x\rjunk"; "Content-Length: 5\njunk\r\n" -> regex length 5, walker 400. Both inputs are invalid per RFC 9112 (the walker's outcome is the RFC-compliant one); neither the test suite, curl, k6 nor the local C generator sends them. Document rather than fix.

4. (b) on the droplet regime every k6 request carries "User-Agent" (10 bytes, same length as "connection"), so the spec walker allocates name+value and runs casecmp? for every GET: k6-style GET measured 590 ns regex vs 490 ns spec walker (a wash within noise), vs 290 ns with a first-letter pre-check. The local generator sends only "Host:", which is why the spec's 0.385->0.198 us GET figure looks better than what the droplet will see.

5. Expected gain is optimistic: weighting measured per-request savings by the mix (83% GET, 15% like, 2% create) gives ~0.6 us headers + ~0.15 us respond + ~0.17 us JWT (after re-adding the 0.3 us alphabet check) + ~0.23 us TRIM + ~0 for the bind-reset trim = ~1.1 us/req, about 1.0% of the 110.4 us baseline, not 1.5%. That is inside the paired-bench noise, so read the bench as "no regression" evidence rather than proof of gain. All numbers are arm64; the x86 regex/Ruby ratio may differ.

Everything else checks out: (a) bytes and encoding (UTF-8) identical, 6->3 allocations, 254->125 ns small / 824->658 ns 2 KB response; (c) premise verified (no JS whitespace char violates the first/last-byte rule; the json 3.1.0 parser rejects lone surrogates with ParserError, so no invalid-UTF-8 string ever reaches gsub and the 500-vs-201 divergence I feared cannot happen), gsub costs 11.5 us per 500-char body vs 0.23 us; (d) extralite 3.1.3 query.c: query_bind calls sqlite3_reset before binding and Query_bind sets should_reset=1, Query_perform_next calls query_reset when set, so the leading reset is a pure no-op (gain negligible, <0.1 us); (e) libsodium 1.0.22 exposes all five functions, statebytes=208, template MAC == one-shot MAC, HMAC alone 1.55->1.1 us, 3-call FFI overhead included. The precomputed ipad/opad state is key schedule, not a verification cache, so rule 5 is respected. HEADER/TRAILING_BLANKS are referenced nowhere outside http.rb.
tech.spec_fixes:
(e) Keep an alphabet guard: before decoding, `raise Halt.new(401, INVALID_TOKEN) if header.match?(/[+\/=]/, 7)` (one pass over the token, measured 285 ns; the three per-segment BASE64URL.match? calls cost 875 ns). With that guard m0's remaining strictness (bad chars, bad padding, non-zero trailing bits) matches the old decode64 exactly, the 43-char signature always decodes to exactly 32 bytes, and the crypto_verify_32 over-read disappears. Net JWT saving becomes ~1.0 us per POST instead of ~1.15. Add to the hand tests: signature with "/" or "+" (expect 401), payload with "=" padding at length % 4 == 0 (expect 401).

(b) Memoize the colon search with a sentinel so the buffer is scanned for a colon at most once per drain: `colon = (buffer.byteindex(COLON, pos) || head_end) if colon.nil? || colon < pos` (initialise `colon = nil` before the loop; the `colon < eol` test then naturally skips lines past the last colon). Measured: pathological case 33 ms -> 0.1 ms, common path unchanged.

(b) Slice name/value only after a first-letter pre-check so k6's User-Agent (10 bytes) never allocates: `letter = buffer.getbyte(pos) | 0x20` and require (14, 'c'=0x63), (17, 't'=0x74), (10, 'c'=0x63), (13, 'a'=0x61) before the byteslice calls; keep the casecmp? afterwards. Measured k6-style GET 490 -> 290 ns, k6 POST 2.2 -> 1.4-2.1 us, allocations 7 -> 3 on a k6 GET.

(b) Replace the "byte-equivalent to the regex" wording with: equivalent for all well-formed heads; for a bare CR/LF inside a field value the walker keeps the whole line as the value (so a Content-Length with trailing junk becomes 400 instead of being silently truncated), which is the RFC 9112 behaviour.

Expected gain: state ~1% (measured components sum to ~1.1 us/req of 110.4 us), confidence "medium" on the paired bench because that is within harness noise; keep "high" only for "no regression". Note the local generator's GET carries a single Host header while the droplet's k6 carries Host/User-Agent/Accept-Encoding, so the k6-style head must be in the micro-benchmark corpus. Benchmark scripts used: <scratchpad>/{bench_respond.rb,bench_headers.rb,bench_headers3.rb,bench_headers4.rb,bench_trim.rb,bench_hmac.rb,probe_b64b.rb} (run with: docker run --rm -v "<scratchpad>:/mb:ro" -w /app -e RUBY_YJIT_ENABLE=1 tdsc-cicloid:base /opt/ruby/bin/bundle exec /opt/ruby/bin/ruby --yjit --yjit-call-threshold=5 /mb/<script>).

ranked_variants.title: Worker pool: LIFO idle stack with direct scheduler push/transfer, 64 resident workers, shrink after bursts, pool diagnostics
ranked_variants.spec:
Files: submissions/ruby-async-cicloid/http.rb and server.rb. Implemented against the unmodified submission (service and its IO::Buffer first read stay as they are).

1. Hand-off. In `run` (63-75): replace `@ready = Thread::Queue.new; @workers = @waiting = 0` with `@idle = []` (LIFO stack of Worker structs), `@backlog = []` (fds that found no idle worker at MAX_WORKERS), `@workers = 0`, `@shrink = 0`. Add `Worker = Struct.new(:fiber, :fd, :io_buffer)`. `WORKERS = 64` (was 256), `MAX_WORKERS = 4096` unchanged.
   `work`: `worker = Worker.new(Fiber.current, nil, IO::Buffer.new(READ_SIZE)); while true; if @shrink > 0 then @shrink -= 1; @workers -= 1; return end; fd = @backlog.shift; unless fd; @idle.push(worker); Fiber.scheduler.transfer; fd = worker.fd; end; begin; service(fd, worker.io_buffer); rescue StandardError => error; Console.error(self, error); end; end`.
   `dispatch` IDLE branch: `@state[fd] = BUSY; if (worker = @idle.pop) then worker.fd = fd; Fiber.scheduler.push(worker.fiber) elsif @workers < MAX_WORKERS then add_worker; worker = @idle.pop; worker.fd = fd; Fiber.scheduler.push(worker.fiber) else @backlog.push(fd) end` (Async runs a new task synchronously up to its first suspension, so after `add_worker` the new worker is already on @idle; assert that and fall back to @backlog if not). IMPORTANT: push every ready fd's worker inside the same dispatch pass (one `Fiber.scheduler.push` per fd), never a chain wake where one worker wakes the next: the chain variant was measured to collapse group-commit batches (commits per 10k likes 116 -> 1100) because only one worker is runnable when the batch leader yields. With per-fd push all workers of a pass are runnable together, exactly as Thread::Queue#push did (it called Scheduler#unblock per push), so batching is unchanged.

2. Shrink. `def trim_workers; surplus = @idle.size - WORKERS; @shrink = surplus if surplus > 0; end` - call it once per second from the existing timer in server.rb (`sleep 1; store.checkpoint; server.trim_workers`). Only idle workers exit (one at a time as they come back to the top of their loop), so a burst never thrashes; growth path is unchanged.

3. Diagnostics (keep; one stderr line every 10 s from the same timer): `workers=#{@workers} idle=#{@idle.size} backlog=#{@backlog.size} minor_gc=#{GC.stat(:minor_gc_count)} gc_ms=#{GC.stat(:time)}`. Interpretation: if `workers` never exceeds ~300 in a 20k/80k run, the shrink path is moot and the remaining gain is locality + fewer fiber roots (each suspended fiber is re-marked on every minor GC: measured 0.5-1.2 ms pause at 0 fibers, 1.5 ms at 256, 6.9 ms at 4096).

Edge cases: exceptions in service must not lose the worker (rescue inside the loop); `@workers` accounting on exit; a worker on the stack is suspended at `transfer`, so `Fiber.scheduler.push(fiber)` must only be called for fibers popped from @idle (never twice). Shutdown: nothing special, as today.

Verify: test/test.sh 42/42; a 20k run with the diagnostic line captured (pool size over time, GC count vs base); paired 20k and 80k runs (p95/p99 too - minor GC pause shrinks with fewer live fibers). Expected per-primitive hand-off cost is a wash (Thread::Queue 1.35-1.50 vs LIFO+push 1.45 us/job); the gain is cache-warm stacks, 192 fewer resident fibers to mark, and bounded pool growth.
ranked_variants.why_ranked_here: The hand-off primitive itself is a wash by micro-measurement, so this is really a pool-size/locality/GC-root experiment; the measured 1.5 us per suspended fiber per minor GC makes it worth one slot, but it conflicts with v02/v10/v11 in http.rb and its gain depends on whether the pool actually grows under the bench, which the diagnostic settles.

rules.problems:
No rule violation found. The variant changes only the fiber hand-off (Thread::Queue -> LIFO stack + Fiber.scheduler.push/transfer), the resident pool size (256 -> 64), a once-a-second trim hook and a stderr diagnostic line. Nothing touches app.rb: every request still reads SQLite, every JWT is still HMAC-verified, pragmas (WAL, synchronous=NORMAL, group commit with each response waiting on its COMMIT promise) and response bytes are unchanged, no kernel tuning, build still from source (rb layer only), server up in ~1 s. The only per-worker state kept across requests is the IO::Buffer, which is overwritten per read and read only up to `length` (same as the baseline), not a data cache.

API check against async 2.46.0 / io-event 1.22.1 in the image: Async::Scheduler#transfer (-> selector.transfer -> loop fiber), #push (-> selector ready queue, exactly what #unblock does minus the wakeup) and #resume all exist and are public; Task#async runs the child greedily until its first suspension, with the caller re-queued as an optional ready entry; IO_Event_Selector_URing_select flushes the ready queue first, so all workers pushed in one dispatch pass run together (group-commit batching preserved). Workers are entered via fiber transfer, so transfer-suspension is legal (identical to Scheduler#block).

Empirical: I implemented the spec literally in local-bench/variants/ref-v06 (image tdsc-cicloid:ref-v06). test/test.sh: passed=42 failed=0. 20k users / 60 s / ramp 20: 126,783 requests, 0 errors, 56.8 us/req, 12.1% CPU, p50 0.85 / p95 4.9 / p99 17.6 ms, 171 MB; pool diagnostics stayed at workers=64-66, idle=57-66, backlog=0, no exceptions logged. A paired same-slot base run right after: 56.5 us/req, 12.1% CPU, p95 4.4 / p99 18.3 ms, 178 MB -> a wash on CPU as the spec itself predicts. Note the 110.4 us/req base figure in the task text is stale (base runs in results/ range 46-110 us/req depending on host conditions); only paired runs (local-bench/pair.sh) are meaningful.

Robustness hazards (not rule breaches, but each can kill the dispatch task and then nothing is served, which would fail a bench): (1) In the growth branch `add_worker; worker = @idle.pop` returns nil whenever @shrink > 0 (the fresh worker exits at the top of its loop before pushing itself) or @backlog is non-empty (the fresh worker takes a backlog fd synchronously). If the "assert" is a raise, dispatch dies. (2) With a stale @shrink counter, returning workers exit before shifting @backlog, delaying backlogged connections. (3) The spec's claim "only idle workers exit" is inaccurate: @shrink is consumed by the hot workers that just finished a job, so shrink digs into the LIFO stack and retires the warmest workers first; the cold ones at the stack bottom (the GC-root cost the variant targets) are never the ones retired.
rules.spec_fixes:
1. Growth path must be a real nil-check, never a raise: `worker = @idle.pop; if !worker && @workers < MAX_WORKERS then @shrink = 0; add_worker; worker = @idle.pop end; if worker then worker.fd = fd; Fiber.scheduler.push(worker.fiber) else @backlog.push(fd) end`. Resetting @shrink = 0 before growing removes the fresh-worker-exits-immediately case.
2. In `work`, check the backlog before the shrink counter: `fd = @backlog.shift; if fd.nil? && @shrink > 0 then @shrink -= 1; @workers -= 1; return end`, so a stale shrink never delays a backlogged connection.
3. Preferred simplification (optional, removes @shrink entirely and retires the coldest fibers, which is the stated goal): `def trim_workers; while @idle.size > WORKERS; worker = @idle.shift; worker.fd = nil; Fiber.scheduler.push(worker.fiber); end; end` and in `work`, after `Fiber.scheduler.transfer`, `fd = worker.fd or begin @workers -= 1; return end`. shift removes the worker from @idle, so the "push only fibers popped from @idle, never twice" invariant still holds, and the growth path can no longer see a nil pop (a fresh worker always pushes itself before transferring).
4. `trim_workers` and the diagnostics accessor (e.g. `stats`) must be public; keep `work`/`dispatch`/`add_worker` private. GC.stat(:time) is available (printed gc_ms in the run).
5. Measurement: compare with local-bench/pair.sh against tdsc-cicloid:base on the same host conditions, not with the 110.4 us/req figure; same-slot base today is 56.5 us/req at 20k, equal to the variant, so expect gains, if any, only in the 80k churn run via GC pause (fewer live fibers) rather than CPU/req.
Evidence paths: <repo>/local-bench/variants/ref-v06 (http.rb, server.rb), .../local-bench/results/ref-v06.jsonl, ref-v06.log (pool lines), ref-v06-base.jsonl.

tech.problems:
No blocker found; the variant is API-correct and does not slow the common path, but its stated rationale is mostly unmeasurable and the measured gain is within noise.

APIs (verified in /app/vendor/bundle/ruby/4.0.0/gems/{async-2.46.0,io-event-1.22.1} inside tdsc-cicloid:base): Async::Scheduler#push(fiber) -> selector.push (xmalloc ready-queue entry, FIFO; entries queued during a flush run in the next flush), #transfer -> loop fiber, #resume(fiber) pushes the caller at the FIFO tail then transfers into the target; Task#schedule uses resume, so `@task.async { work }` inside dispatch runs the new worker synchronously until it parks (so `@idle.pop` right after add_worker always succeeds because that branch is only entered when @idle was empty) and dispatch itself resumes only in the NEXT reactor iteration — growth costs one loop pass per worker. Same as the base's add_worker, so not a regression. Thread::Queue#push under the scheduler is exactly one `unblock` = one `push`, so the base is already "one push per fd per pass"; the no-chain-wake rule is a property of both designs, not a gain. io_read (RUBY_FIBER_SCHEDULER_VERSION>=4) does an optimistic read() first, so a worker almost never suspends inside service(); the LIFO stack therefore mostly holds workers in park order, which is what the spec assumes.

Measurements (local harness, Docker arm64, paired runs on separate cpusets):
- 20k users/60s: ref-v06 56.8 us/req vs base 56.5 us/req, p95 4.9 vs 4.4 ms, p99 17.6 vs 18.3 ms, 171 vs 178 MB -> wash. At 20k the base pool never grows past 256 and the variant stays at 64-66 workers, so shrink is moot at this load.
- 80k users/60s, two paired runs (second with swapped start order): variant 41.5 / 41.3 us/req vs base 43.7 / 41.8; CPU 35.0/35.0 vs 36.9/35.3 %; p99 131 vs 49 ms and 30 vs 26 ms (mixed); peak RSS 391/386 vs 394/396 MB. Gain is 0.5-5 %, inside run-to-run noise (earlier base 80k runs: 63.7 and 69.1 us/req). Memory saving is 1-2 %: RSS is dominated by 65k open connections, not by 300-460 fibers.
- Group commit: commit counters were identical in both pairs (21.5k/21.5k and 21.3k/21.4k commits per run; 1600-1800 per 5 s in every window), so trimming to 64 does NOT shrink group-commit batches — the batch is bounded by ready fds per pass, which the regrown pool covers. (This refutes the concern that trim would re-split batches.)
- Base pool at 80k grows to 337-461 workers (not ~1150; that earlier figure came from a noisy run) and never shrinks; variant oscillates 119 -> 315 -> 144 -> 123 -> 186 every second: trim to 64, then regrow 100-250 workers, each regrowth step = fiber create + a loop yield of dispatch. Cost is small (CPU not worse) but it is pure churn with no measured benefit; WORKERS=64 is below the steady-state need at 80k (119-315 workers in use).
- Hand-off micro-benchmark: LIFO array + scheduler.push 0.57-0.58 us/job vs Thread::Queue 0.80-0.97 us/job -> ~0.3 us per request (0.3-0.5 % of a 60-110 us request). Spec calls this a wash; it is in fact the only part of the gain that is demonstrable.
- Locality: real parser+app+SQLite path, FIFO over 256 fibers 116.39 us vs LIFO 116.20 us (round 0), 152.65 vs 163.66 (round 2) -> no demonstrable cache-warm-stack gain on this harness.
- GC: minor GC pause scales ~1.2 us per suspended fiber (74 us @0, 116 @64, 268 @256, 1153 @1024, 4943 @4096). At 0.7-1.2 minor GC/s under load, 256 -> 64 workers saves ~0.2-0.3 ms/s of CPU, i.e. <0.1 %; gc_ms in the paired runs is the same (1103 vs 1168, 1086 vs 1269 ms over the run, noise).

Design nits (not blockers): the `@shrink` check sits at the top of the work loop, so the worker that exits is the one that was just popped from the LIFO top (the warm one) after it finishes one more service, while cold bottom-of-stack workers survive — the inverse of the locality rationale. `@shrink` is a stale counter: it must be reset to 0 on growth (ref-v06 does) and would otherwise keep killing workers during the burst that follows a trim. The backlog branch (MAX_WORKERS=4096) is never exercised (backlog=0 in every sample) but is a necessary bound. No challenge-rule risk: pool sizing is process-internal, trim is a fixed timer (no load detection), service()/response bytes unchanged (42/42 unaffected), no caching, durability untouched.
tech.spec_fixes:
1. Replace the `@shrink` counter with bottom-of-stack eviction in trim_workers: `surplus.times { w = @idle.shift; w.fd = nil; Fiber.scheduler.push(w.fiber) }`, and in `work`: after `fd = worker.fd`, `if fd.nil? then @workers -= 1; return end`. This evicts the cold workers (keeps the LIFO-warm ones), removes the stale-counter state and the need to reset `@shrink` on growth, and costs at most one flush of fiber exits per second (~250 exits, <1 ms). If the counter design is kept, keep the `@shrink = 0` reset in the growth path and state it explicitly in the spec.
2. Add hysteresis so the pool does not oscillate 64 <-> 300 every second at 80k: trim toward max(WORKERS, peak idle over the last ~5 s / 2), or evict at most ~32 per tick, or raise WORKERS to 128-256 (steady-state need at 80k is 119-315). Keep MAX_WORKERS=4096 as the bound.
3. Correct the expected-gain narrative: the hand-off is the measurable part (~0.3 us/req, LIFO+push 0.57 us/job vs Thread::Queue 0.80-0.97 us/job), not "a wash"; locality and GC marking are not measurable on the real path (116.4 vs 116.2 us; <0.1 % CPU); memory effect is ~1-2 % RSS at 80k (386-391 vs 394-396 MB). State expected gain as "<=1 % CPU, 1-2 % RSS; 20k: wash; 80k: 0.5-5 % within noise".
4. Add a `commits` counter to Store (increment before `batch.resolve`) and print it in the diagnostics line next to workers/idle/backlog/open, so a reviewer can verify group-commit batch size is unchanged (it was: identical commit counts in both paired runs).
5. The assertion after add_worker should be `!@idle.empty?` (true because the branch is only entered when `@idle.pop` returned nil and the new worker parks synchronously), with `@backlog.push(fd)` as the fallback; do not phrase it as "the new worker is on top", which depends on scheduler semantics.
6. Evaluate the variant at 80k users (pool never grows at 20k, so shrink is moot there) with paired/concurrent runs on separate cpusets; report us/req, CPU %, RSS, p99, pool min/max and commits per window.

ranked_variants.title: Profile-guided Ruby build (two-pass PGO trained on the server's own request path)
ranked_variants.spec:
Files: submissions/ruby-async-cicloid/install.sh (the Ruby configure/make at lines 70-71) plus a new training script ruby_train.rb next to it; local-bench/Dockerfile must COPY ruby_train.rb into the first layer alongside install.sh and sqlite_train.c (the layer that runs install.sh). A working reference already exists at local-bench/variants/rt-pgo/{install.sh (lines 72-91), ruby_train.rb}, image tdsc-cicloid:rt-pgo, build log in the judge's scratchpad micro/build-rt-pgo.log; reuse it.

Pass 1: `./configure --prefix=$work/ruby-instrumented --enable-yjit --with-jemalloc --disable-install-doc --disable-install-rdoc cflags="$NATIVE" XCFLAGS="-fprofile-generate -fprofile-update=atomic -fprofile-dir=$work/rbpgo" LDFLAGS="-fprofile-generate"`, make -j, make install; install the pinned gems into that prefix (`gem install extralite:3.1.3 -- --with-sqlite3-dir=/opt/sqlite`, then async:2.46.0 io-event:1.22.1 rbnacl:7.1.2 json:3.1.0 ffi:1.17.4); `rm -rf $work/rbpgo`; run `$work/ruby-instrumented/bin/ruby --yjit --yjit-call-threshold=5 ruby_train.rb $work/train-ruby.db` - the trainer builds a synthetic DB with the sqlite_train.c schema, forks a 64-connection keep-alive client and serves ~51k reactor requests in the bench mix (46% feed, 46% post, 7% like, 1% create, with JWT verification) through the real http.rb/app.rb/server.rb, then exits normally (no exit!, or no .gcda is written). Pass 2: configure for /opt/ruby with XCFLAGS="-fprofile-use -fprofile-partial-training -fprofile-dir=$work/rbpgo -Wno-missing-profile" and a `-Werror=missing-profile` gate on the core objects so an empty profile fails the build; make, make install; then build.sh as today installs the gems against the final ruby.

Constraints: install must still complete inside the challenge's install budget on 1 vCPU (two Ruby compiles + 1-2 min training; measure the wall time and report it); the training script must not touch the real DB or port. If the profiled app files change later (v02-v06), the profile remains valid (partial training keeps un-profiled code normally optimised).

Verify: `readelf -S /opt/ruby/bin/ruby` .text size differs from base (rt-pgo: 0x4ab4bc vs base 0x4cfd3c); test/test.sh 42/42; paired 20k bench (prior interleaved n=5 micro: 24.34 -> 23.02 us/req min, about -5% of userland).
ranked_variants.why_ranked_here: Only toolchain item with a measured interleaved win (n=5) and an existing working build; it is orthogonal to every rb change. Ranked mid-list because the gain is ~1% of total and the install-time cost on the 1-vCPU target still needs confirming.

rules.problems:
No concrete rule violation found. Evidence: (1) app.rb/http.rb/server.rb/epoll.rb/build.sh/start.sh/Gemfile* in local-bench/variants/rt-pgo are byte-identical to the submission (diff -q), so rules 2/3/5/6 (SQLite-only, fixed schema, no cross-request caching, JWT verified per request, WAL + synchronous=NORMAL, group commit waits for COMMIT) are untouched; PGO only changes the interpreter's machine code. (2) Rule 4: I ran test/test.sh against tdsc-cicloid:rt-pgo (bench.sh --test, name v07ref-test): passed=42 failed=0, server up after 2 s. (3) Rule 10: everything is compiled on the box; the .gcda profile is generated during install.sh and discarded with $work; the final /opt/ruby/bin/ruby and libruby-static.a have 0 gcov symbols and no .gcda strings; rbconfig CFLAGS/XCFLAGS/LDFLAGS are identical to base (only configure_args records the XCFLAGS string, which mkmf does not use), so gems built by build.sh are unaffected. (4) Rule 7: training on the request mix is the same technique the accepted base already uses for SQLite (sqlite_train.c, README lines 67-71); behaviour does not depend on the workload and there is no load-test detection. (5) Rule 11: a compiler flag on our own binary, not a box setting. (6) Training touches only $work/train-ruby.db and 127.0.0.1:3100-4099, never $SQLITE_PATH or the service port.

Wrong assumptions / spec defects that would bite as written:
A. Verification numbers are swapped: measured base .text = 0x4ab4bc, rt-pgo .text = 0x4cfd3c (the PGO binary is the larger one).
B. The Dockerfile instruction is insufficient and would fail the build: ruby_train.rb does require_relative "app" and "http" (http.rb requires epoll.rb), which the harness Dockerfile only copies in the final `COPY . /app/`. Adding only ruby_train.rb to the first COPY leaves `bash /app/install.sh` failing with LoadError at the training step. The existing tdsc-cicloid:rt-pgo image was NOT built with local-bench/Dockerfile: its history is a single layer `cp -R /src/. /app/ && bash install.sh && bash build.sh`.
C. The `-Werror=missing-profile gate on the core objects` does not exist in the reference (lines 87-88 use -Wno-missing-profile) and cannot be applied per object through Ruby's Makefile without failing on un-exercised TUs (enc/*, ext/openssl, ripper). The reference's actual gate is `test -n "$(ls -A "$pgo")"`, which is weak: the forked client's exit status is never checked, so a client failure (connect timeout, exception in the child) leaves the parent exiting 0 with a warm-up-only profile and the build proceeds.
D. Training fidelity: `gem install async:2.46.0 io-event:1.22.1 ...` resolved and loaded io-event 1.22.3 (build log: /gems/io-event-1.22.3/lib/IO_Event.so), not the pinned 1.22.1, and ffi arrived as the prebuilt platform gem (ffi-1.17.4-aarch64-linux-gnu; x86_64 equivalent on the droplet) whereas build.sh forces the ruby platform. Nothing is shipped (prefix deleted), so no rule-10 issue, but the trainer does not match production. In the Docker build io_uring was unavailable ("Operation not permitted"), so the local profile was trained on the epoll selector; on the droplet (root, no seccomp) it will train on io_uring.
E. Install wall time on 1 vCPU is unmeasured. Only data point: 9.5 min for the whole image on a 10-CPU arm64 Docker Desktop (build log 23:38:34 -> 23:48:09, make -j10). The README's "~10 min on 1 vCPU" covers one Ruby compile; expect roughly 2x plus 1-2 min for instrumented gem builds and training (~20-30 min). No rule sets an install budget (CI runner is 4 vCPU with a 6 h job limit; rule 10's 60 s applies to start.sh and is met at 2 s), but the README claim becomes false.
F. README not updated: the rules require the README to document the optimizations; it currently says "built from source with jemalloc and -march=native" and "~10 min on 1 vCPU".
G. Idempotency: the Ruby block is guarded only by `ruby -e 'print RUBY_VERSION' != 4.0.7`, so a box with a plain 4.0.7 in /opt/ruby silently skips PGO (SQLite uses a "-pgo" VERSION marker; Ruby has none). Clean-box only, so not a violation.
H. Port 3100+rand(1000) can collide on a shared box and abort install; low risk on a clean droplet/CI.
I. Measurement caveat: the n=5 interleaved micro has two base outliers (30.75, 31.43 us/req); min-vs-min is 5.4%, median 7%. The ~1.2% of total is plausible but unconfirmed by the paired 20k bench.
rules.spec_fixes:
1. Swap the verification figures: base .text 0x4ab4bc, rt-pgo .text 0x4cfd3c (PGO is larger, as expected with partial training).
2. Dockerfile: change line 8 to `COPY install.sh sqlite_train.c* ruby_train.rb app.rb http.rb epoll.rb /app/`, and state that this makes the toolchain layer depend on app/http/epoll, so any rb variant stacked on v07 rebuilds the toolchain (two Ruby compiles); or build v07 with the ad-hoc single-layer method the judge used for rt-pgo.
3. Replace the "-Werror=missing-profile gate on the core objects" wording with the real gate and strengthen it: keep -Wno-missing-profile in pass 2; after training require specific hot objects, e.g. `ls "$pgo" | grep -q 'vm\.gcda$' && ls "$pgo" | grep -q 'vm_insnhelper\.gcda$'` (or at least `gc.gcda`, `string.gcda`), and in ruby_train.rb check the client: `Process.wait(client); abort "training client failed" unless $?.success?`. Also guard against a mostly-idle run, e.g. count served requests in the server (or require the client to have completed all ROUNDS before exit!(0)).
4. Pass-1 gem install: use `gem install --no-document --platform ruby -v 1.22.1 io-event` before async (or `gem install ... --conservative` with explicit versions) and `--platform ruby` for ffi, so the trainer runs the same io-event 1.22.1 and source-built ffi as production.
5. Install budget: measure once with `docker run --cpuset-cpus=1 -e ... ubuntu:24.04 bash install.sh` (BuildKit ignores cpuset), report the wall time, and update README's "~10 min on 1 vCPU" to the measured figure.
6. README.md: add a bullet under "Optimizations, and why" describing the two-pass Ruby PGO (instrumented build, ruby_train.rb running the server's own parser/app/reactor over a synthetic DB in the request mix, final build with -fprofile-use -fprofile-partial-training), mirroring the existing SQLite PGO bullet, and change the Language row to mention PGO.
7. Optional robustness: write a marker (e.g. `/opt/ruby/PGO`) and key the Ruby rebuild on it like SQLite's VERSION file; let ruby_train.rb retry a few random ports on EADDRINUSE.
8. Before merging, confirm the gain with the paired 20k bench (the micro's base series has two outliers), and note that the local profile was trained on the epoll selector while the droplet trains on io_uring.

tech.problems:
No demonstrated reason to refuse; the premise holds, but the spec has several factual/feasibility errors:

1. .text figures are swapped. readelf on the images: base .text = 0x4ab4bc, rt-pgo = 0x4cfd3c (PGO GREW .text by ~150 KB, +2.2%, consistent with hot-path inlining/unrolling). The spec says "rt-pgo: 0x4ab4bc vs base 0x4cfd3c".

2. The "-Werror=missing-profile gate on the core objects" is infeasible as a global XCFLAGS flag: XCFLAGS applies to every Ruby object, and after `rm -rf $work/rbpgo` the miniruby-only objects (dmydln.o, miniinit.o, dmyext.o) and every extension not loaded during training have no .gcda, so pass 2 would fail. The reference build that actually succeeded (local-bench/variants/rt-pgo/install.sh lines 69-91, log <session-root>/scratchpad/micro/build-rt-pgo.log) uses only `-Wno-missing-profile` plus `test -n "$(ls -A "$pgo")"`.

3. The Dockerfile fix is incomplete. ruby_train.rb does `require_relative "app"` / `"http"` (and http pulls epoll.rb), so the install layer must COPY app.rb, http.rb and epoll.rb as well as ruby_train.rb. That also means every edit to those files invalidates the toolchain layer (two Ruby builds + training). The existing tdsc-cicloid:rt-pgo image was NOT built through local-bench/Dockerfile but by scratchpad/micro/build-pinned.sh as a single layer on --cpuset-cpus=0 (~13 min on one arm64 core; the base install layer took 3m40s on 10 cores).

4. Training gems are unpinned: `gem install async:2.46.0 ...` resolved and installed io-event 1.22.3 before io-event 1.22.1 (build log lines 3073/3080) and the trainer's `require "async"` activated 1.22.3; ffi arrived as a prebuilt aarch64 platform gem. The shipped runtime (build.sh/Gemfile.lock) is still io-event 1.22.1, so correctness is unaffected, but the profile was not trained on the exact pinned stack and the install step fetches unpinned versions from the network.

5. Evidence/noise: the paired 20k harness bench cannot resolve a 1.2% change (base 20k runs in local-bench/results span 46-110 us/req). The only instrument that resolves it is the in-process interleaved micro: scratchpad/micro/abimg-1793227751.jsonl, n=5 keep-alive, base min 24.34 / med 25.97 vs rt-pgo min 23.02 / med 24.10 us/req, rt-pgo faster in 4/5 pairs (~-5% userland; userland is ~25 of ~110 us/req total, so ~1.2% end-to-end is plausible). Untrained regime: the trainer keeps 64 persistent connections, so accept/close/epoll_ctl paths run only 64 times. My churn micro (one request per connection, scratchpad/v07review/micro_churn.rb, results scratchpad/v07review/abchurn-client-1793232252.jsonl) interleaved n=4 on a contended host: base min 37.24 / med 40.19 vs rt-pgo min 34.62 / med 42.11, 2/4 pairs each way. No slowdown demonstrated, but no gain either; -fprofile-partial-training keeps untrained functions at plain -O3, which is why no regression is expected there.

6. Install cost is undocumented: two full Ruby builds + 51k-request training. Measured ~13 min total on one arm64 core (apt + SQLite PGO + libsodium + 2x Ruby + gems + training + build.sh). README sets no install budget (only "healthy within 60 s of start.sh", which is unaffected: the final binary carries no instrumentation), but on the judge's 1-vCPU x86_64 box expect roughly 2x the base install wall time.
