With the chain-wake hand-off that is a single worker (commits per 10k like requests: 116 -> 1100); with the loop it is every worker that becomes runnable while members keep arriving (50 per 10k, i.e. 4x fewer transactions than the current baseline's 207). Each avoided transaction saves BEGIN/COMMIT overhead in SQLite, the WAL commit frame pwrite and an fstat, and lets inserts into the same pages share WAL frames. Measured CPU effect locally is within noise (r3y vs r3: mix 28.9 vs 29.1, like 25.5 vs 24.9 us), so the gain estimate rests on the Xeon profile (SQLite 15% of CPU, of which commit/WAL bookkeeping is a fraction) at ~8% POSTs.
all_proposals.correctness_risk: Low. Responses are still sent only after COMMIT returns, so durability (synchronous=NORMAL WAL as today) is unchanged. Without the rounds cap a sustained POST stream could delay a commit by several reactor passes; the cap bounds it. Each extra yield costs ~1.2 us for the leader fiber per joining member, which is why it is neutral on CPU locally.
all_proposals.rule_risk: none (writes remain durable before the response; nothing is cached across requests)

all_proposals.title: After servicing a batch, re-poll epoll with timeout 0 before parking in poller.wait_readable
all_proposals.change: http.rb `dispatch` (lines 121-137): change the loop to `loop do; n = Epoll.ready(@epfd, events, MAX_EVENTS) { |fd| ... same body ... }; if n.zero? then poller.wait_readable else task-yield once (`Fiber.scheduler.yield` / `@task.yield`) so the woken workers service the batch before the next non-blocking poll end; end` (Epoll.ready must return the event count; if it does not, have it return the epoll_wait result). Net effect: a dispatch pass only goes through the io_uring POLL_ADD / CQE / fiber round trip when the previous non-blocking epoll_wait came back empty.
all_proposals.rationale: Each `poller.wait_readable` is an io_wait SQE + enter + CQE + two fiber transfers (~3-4 us), taken once per dispatch pass; the README's 40k-user profile shows ~5.6 requests per epoll_wait, i.e. under saturation events are almost always pending when a pass ends. An empty epoll_wait(0) through the FFI shim costs 0.39 us and a task.yield 1.24 us, so when the backlog was non-empty the re-poll saves 2-3 us per pass (~0.4 us/req at 5.6 req/pass) and costs ~1.6 us per pass when it comes back empty (idle, light load). NOT measured end-to-end; the estimate is arithmetic on the micro numbers and the README's pass size.
all_proposals.correctness_risk: Low. Edge-triggered semantics unchanged (edges are not lost; the epoll fd is simply read again). Adds one yield per pass; under light load it is a small loss, so gate it on `n > 0`. Needs an A/B at the bench's connection count before adoption.

all_proposals.title: Build the response with a single interpolated String instead of String.new(capacity:) + three appends
all_proposals.change: http.rb `respond` (lines 283-288): replace `out = String.new(head, capacity: ...); out << document.bytesize.to_s << END_HEAD << document; write(socket, out)` with `write(socket, "#{head}#{document.bytesize}\r\n\r\n#{document}")`. (A per-worker reusable `out` buffer with `clear` would save one more object but requires threading the buffer into drain/respond; the write SQE completes before the fiber resumes, so reuse is safe, but the extra plumbing is not worth 0.04 us.)
all_proposals.rationale: Micro: current assembly 1.37 us / 4 objects per response, interpolation 1.17 us / 2 objects, reusable buffer 1.13 us / 1 object. Saves ~0.2 us and two allocations per response; everything else on the response path (frozen head tables keyed by status, prebuilt END_HEAD) is already minimal.
all_proposals.correctness_risk: None observable: identical bytes on the wire.

all_proposals.title: Drop the ORDER BY inside group_concat in Store::FEED (removes a temp B-tree sort per /feed)
all_proposals.change:
In submissions/ruby-async-cicloid/app.rb, class Store, replace the FEED constant with:

FEED = "SELECT '{\"posts\":['||coalesce(group_concat(doc,','),'')||']}' " \
       "FROM (SELECT #{POST_JSON} AS doc FROM posts p JOIN users u ON u.id=p.user_id " \
       "ORDER BY p.created_at DESC,p.id DESC LIMIT 20)"

i.e. remove `ORDER BY created_at DESC,id DESC` from the group_concat call and drop the now-unused `p.created_at,p.id` columns from the subquery. Nothing else changes (same prepared statement, same `@feed.reset.next; @feed.reset` call pattern). Optional safety net: at Store#initialize run both the old and the new statement once and `abort` if the documents differ, so a future SQLite bump that changed the plan would fail health rather than reorder the feed.
all_proposals.rationale: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN of the current FEED shows `USE TEMP B-TREE FOR group_concat(ORDER BY)`: SQLite builds a sorter, inserts 20 records of ~250 bytes (doc + two keys), sorts and reads them back on every feed. Without the aggregate ORDER BY the plan is `CO-ROUTINE (subquery-2) / SCAN p USING INDEX posts_created_at_id_idx / SEARCH u ... / CORRELATED SCALAR SUBQUERY / SCAN (subquery-2)` with no sorter: the aggregate consumes the co-routine rows in index order (created_at DESC, id DESC, LIMIT 20), so the order is preserved by construction. Measured in the image (prepared, next+reset, 10k iterations, three separate runs): 32.6->? not run; 64.0 -> 50.2 us (-21%), 70.4 -> 52.8 us (-25%), 39.0 -> 24.1 us (-38%). Output is byte-equal to the current FEED on the seed DB (5102-byte document, verified with ==). The feed is 1 of every 2.17 requests (46%), and the feed query is ~30% of the 110 us/req baseline, so -12..-15 us per feed is roughly -6 us per request on average. Variant with LIMIT applied before the users join (SELECT ... FROM (top-20 subquery) p JOIN users u) measured the same within noise (23.5 vs 24.1 us), so keep the minimal change. Replacing json_object with || and json_quote was slower (82 vs 64 us): discard.
all_proposals.correctness_risk: SQLite documents group_concat order as arbitrary without ORDER BY; here it is fixed by the plan (co-routine over an ordered LIMIT subquery, no sorter) and SQLite is statically linked at a pinned version (3.54), so the plan cannot drift at runtime. test/test.sh line 121 checks the new post is posts[0]; ties on created_at are still broken by id DESC inside the subquery. Cross-lens item (SQL text lives in app.rb but the cost is SQLite): worth a second look from the SQLite lens, and a byte-compare against the old statement at boot costs nothing.
all_proposals.rule_risk: none (no caching, schema untouched, bytes identical)

all_proposals.title: Group commit without a Task/Promise per batch: first writer of the pass yields once and commits; waiters park with Fiber.scheduler.block/unblock
all_proposals.change:
In app.rb class Store: (1) prepare the transaction statements once in initialize: `@begin = @db.prepare("BEGIN IMMEDIATE"); @commit = @db.prepare("COMMIT")`. (2) Replace Async::Promise with a tiny waiter list:

class Batch
  def initialize; @waiters = []; @done = false; @error = nil; end
  def wait
    unless @done
      @waiters << Fiber.current
      Fiber.scheduler.block(self, nil)
    end
    raise @error if @error
    true
  end
  def resolve!(error = nil)
    @done = true; @error = error
    waiters, @waiters = @waiters, nil
    scheduler = Fiber.scheduler
    waiters.each { |fiber| scheduler.unblock(self, fiber) }
  end
end

(3) Replace begin_batch + the `Async do |task| task.yield; commit(batch) end` with a leader pattern used by create and like:

def write
  if (batch = @batch)
    result = yield
    batch.wait
    return result
  end
  @begin.execute
  batch = @batch = Batch.new
  begin
    yield
  ensure
    Fiber.scheduler.yield   # let every request already ready in this pass join the batch
    commit(batch)
  end
end

def like(user_id, post_id)
  write do
    outcome = if @like.execute(user_id, post_id) == 1 then :liked
              elsif @exists.reset.bind(post_id).next then :already_liked
              else :missing end
    @exists.reset
    outcome
  end
end
# create: same shape around the RETURNING statement

def commit(batch)
  @batch = nil
  begin
    @commit.execute
  rescue Extralite::Error => error
    @db.execute("ROLLBACK") if @db.transaction_active?
    return batch.resolve!(error)
  end
  batch.resolve!
  checkpoint! if @checkpoint_due
end

Reads keep `@batch&.wait`. Semantics are unchanged: BEGIN IMMEDIATE on the first write of a pass, every request ready in that pass joins, one COMMIT on the next pass, every write response (and the leader's own) is sent only after COMMIT returned; a rejected batch raises in every waiter. The alternative measured (a single long-lived committer task parked with Fiber.scheduler.transfer and woken by Fiber.scheduler.push(fiber) from begin_batch, created with Async(transient: true) from server.rb) works too but costs one extra fiber switch per batch; prefer the leader.
all_proposals.rationale: Today every batch allocates an Async::Task + Fiber + Async::Promise (Mutex + ConditionVariable) and the waiter path goes through ConditionVariable#wait -> scheduler block. Quiet-run micro numbers in the image (YJIT): `task.async {}` spawn 5.6 us / 21 objects, spawn+yield+wait 7.75 us / 23 objects, Promise spawn-resolver+wait 8.6 us / 26 objects, versus a block/unblock or push/transfer round trip of ~1-2 us. Allocation drop is certain and reproducible: sequential Store#like 27 -> 5 objects per request, App#call POST like 55.6 -> 33.6 objects (fewer minor GCs). At 20k users there are at most ~170 batches/s against ~2170 req/s, so ~6 us saved per batch is ~0.5 us per request (0.4%); the share grows with load because batches get bigger but the cost per batch is fixed, so the saving per request actually shrinks at saturation. Interleaved end-to-end A/B/C runs in my harness (as-is vs committer fiber vs leader) did not resolve a difference above WAL/I-O noise: sequential like means 54.0/53.9/54.2 us (p50 42.5/41.9/39.6), App#call POST like means 38.8/28.8/25.5 us, mixed per-pass results. So the gain is inferred from components, not proven end to end. Replacing group commit with an inline COMMIT per write was measured and is worse (+21 us per write, 67.5 vs 46.3 us): keep batching.
all_proposals.correctness_risk: The leader must commit from `ensure` so a raising statement (e.g. the FK/constraint error path) never leaves BEGIN IMMEDIATE open with parked followers; Batch#wait must raise the commit error for every waiter; Task#stop on a leader parked at Fiber.scheduler.yield still runs ensure. Fiber.scheduler.block/unblock are the public scheduler API (unblock pushes + wakeup, safe from the same thread). Run test/test.sh (42/42) plus a forced COMMIT failure test (e.g. simulate by raising in commit) before adopting.
all_proposals.rule_risk: none: every write still waits for its own COMMIT before the response is written (WAL + synchronous=NORMAL unchanged)

all_proposals.title: LIKE as a plain VALUES upsert; let the existing FOREIGN KEY reject missing posts instead of INSERT..SELECT WHERE EXISTS
all_proposals.change:
In app.rb class Store replace

LIKE = "INSERT INTO likes(user_id,post_id) SELECT ?1,?2 WHERE EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM posts WHERE id=?2) ON CONFLICT(user_id,post_id) DO NOTHING"

with

LIKE = "INSERT INTO likes(user_id,post_id) VALUES(?1,?2) ON CONFLICT(user_id,post_id) DO NOTHING"

and make Store#like:

def like(user_id, post_id)
  batch = begin_batch
  outcome = begin
    @like.execute(user_id, post_id) == 1 ? :liked : :already_liked
  rescue Extralite::Error => error
    # FK failure on a missing post: statement already rolled back, batch transaction still open
    raise error if @exists.reset.bind(post_id).next
    :missing
  ensure
    @exists.reset
  end
  batch.wait
  outcome
end

PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON is already set in Store#initialize and must stay (it is what turns a missing post into an error). user_id comes from the verified JWT, and likes(user_id) also has a FK, so a bogus sub still cannot insert a dangling row.
all_proposals.rationale: With foreign_keys=ON the insert already probes posts(id) for the FK; the EXISTS subquery is a second probe plus the INSERT..SELECT code path (co-routine + upsert check per produced row). Measured interleaved in one long transaction, random user x post, FK on (so both forms see the same page state): current form mean 7.96 us / p50 6.04 us, VALUES form mean 4.48 us / p50 3.13 us, i.e. -3.5 us per successful like; the `INSERT ... SELECT ?1,id FROM posts WHERE id=?2` shape measured the same as the current one (8.0 us), so the cost is the INSERT..SELECT path, not the probe. Already-liked path: 2.09 vs 2.53 us. Missing-post path: 4.4 us (raise + rescue + EXISTS) vs 2.5 us, but that is the 404 path and is not in the load mix. Likes are 0.15/2.17 = 6.9% of requests, so -3.5 us per like is about -0.24 us per request (0.2%).
all_proposals.correctness_risk: Outcomes map 1:1: changes==1 -> :liked (201), changes==0 -> :already_liked (200), FK violation -> :missing (404); a like row for a non-existent post cannot exist (no deletes), so the conflict/missing cases never overlap. FKs in schema.sql are immediate (no DEFERRABLE), so the error is raised at step time; SQLite rolls back only the failed statement and the batch transaction stays open and committable (verified in the image: 5k rescued FK errors inside one BEGIN IMMEDIATE, then COMMIT). The rescue re-raises any other Extralite::Error so real failures still surface as 500. test/test.sh covers 404 on like of a missing post and the already-liked path.

all_proposals.title: Optional, design decision: let GET /feed and GET /posts/:id respond without waiting for an open write batch
all_proposals.change: In app.rb Store#feed and Store#post delete the `@batch&.wait` line (reads then return as soon as the statement has produced its document). Writes keep waiting. If adopted, update the README paragraph that documents 'Reads that run while a batch is open may have seen its rows, so they wait too.'
all_proposals.rationale: A read that lands in a reactor pass with an open batch today pays a scheduler park/resume (Promise#wait -> ConditionVariable -> block, then unblock + push, ~2-3 us in a quiet run) and its response is delayed until after the COMMIT's WAL write (~40 us when likes dirty fresh pages). Measured per pass of 1 like + 8 reads, interleaved: leader design with reads waiting 202 us mean / 174 p50, same design with reads not waiting 158 / 139, as-is 181 / 158. At 20k users few passes contain a write (~170 writes/s against ~1800 passes/s, most passes hold one request), so the CPU effect is ~0.1-0.3%; near saturation almost every pass contains a write and nearly every read parks, where this is worth up to ~2% CPU and a visible p50 drop for reads. Not a rule issue (rule 6 is about write responses) but it does weaken a consistency property cicloid chose on purpose: if a COMMIT fails (disk full, I/O error) a read may already have shown a post or like that never persisted. Listed so the decision is explicit; I would not take it silently.
all_proposals.correctness_risk: Read-your-uncommitted-write becomes visible only when COMMIT fails after the read was answered (phantom post/like for that one response). All exact-byte tests still pass since the read sees the same rows; test/test.sh is unaffected.
all_proposals.rule_risk: none by the letter (durability rule covers write responses); consistency trade-off, flag for the maintainer

all_proposals.title: Leaner authenticate: slice the header once, direct libsodium FFI calls with a precomputed HMAC state, strict base64 decode instead of regex pre-checks, clock_gettime
all_proposals.change:
In app.rb: (1) in module Sodium add `attach_function :crypto_auth_hmacsha256_statebytes, [], :size_t`, `attach_function :crypto_auth_hmacsha256_init, %i[pointer pointer size_t], :int`, `attach_function :crypto_auth_hmacsha256_update, %i[pointer pointer ulong_long], :int`, `attach_function :crypto_auth_hmacsha256_final, %i[pointer pointer], :int` (and keep `crypto_verify_32` attached directly). (2) In App#initialize build the keyed state once: `size = Sodium.crypto_auth_hmacsha256_statebytes; tmpl = FFI::MemoryPointer.new(size); Sodium.crypto_auth_hmacsha256_init(tmpl, @key, 32); @hmac_template = tmpl.get_bytes(0, size); @hmac_state = FFI::MemoryPointer.new(size)` (208 bytes). (3) Rewrite authenticate as:

def authenticate(header)
  raise Halt.new(401, MISSING_TOKEN) unless header&.start_with?("Bearer ")
  size = header.bytesize
  first = header.index(".", 7)
  last = header.rindex(".")
  raise Halt.new(401, INVALID_TOKEN) unless first && first != last && size - last - 1 == 43
  signing = header.byteslice(7, last - 7)            # no .b copy: FFI only needs the bytes
  @hmac_state.put_bytes(0, @hmac_template)           # fresh keyed state, key never re-hashed
  Sodium.crypto_auth_hmacsha256_update(@hmac_state, signing, signing.bytesize)
  Sodium.crypto_auth_hmacsha256_final(@hmac_state, @mac)
  sig = header.byteslice(last + 1, 43)
  sig.tr!("-_", "+/"); sig << "="
  decoded = begin
    sig.unpack1("m0")                                # strict: rejects any non-base64 byte
  rescue ArgumentError
    raise Halt.new(401, INVALID_TOKEN)
  end
  raise Halt.new(401, INVALID_TOKEN) unless Sodium.crypto_verify_32(@mac, decoded) == 0
  head = header.byteslice(7, first - 7)
  unless head == HS256_HEADER
    fields = parse_segment(head)
    raise Halt.new(401, INVALID_TOKEN) unless fields.is_a?(Hash) && fields["alg"] == "HS256"
  end
  seg = header.byteslice(first + 1, last - first - 1)
  seg.tr!("-_", "+/")
  pad = -seg.bytesize % 4
  raise Halt.new(401, INVALID_TOKEN) if pad == 3
  seg << (pad == 1 ? "=" : "==") if pad != 0
  claims = begin
    CODER.load(seg.unpack1("m0"))
  rescue JSON::ParserError, ArgumentError, EncodingError
    raise Halt.new(401, INVALID_TOKEN)
  end
  raise Halt.new(401, INVALID_TOKEN) unless claims.is_a?(Hash)
  now = Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_REALTIME)
  ... exp / nbf / sub / username checks exactly as today ...
end

(4) `CODER = JSON::Coder.new(freeze: true)` (claims are only read). Optional: `OpenSSL.fixed_length_secure_compare(@mac, decoded)` is 59 ns vs 155 ns for crypto_verify_32 but needs `require "openssl"` (~8 MB RSS per the submission README); skip unless memory is irrelevant. Keep the libsodium HMAC: OpenSSL::HMAC is slower (see rationale).
all_proposals.rationale: Quiet-run micro numbers in the image (ns per call / objects): current authenticate 5,110 / 22; the rewrite 3,962 / 14 with the one-shot HMAC, and the precomputed-state HMAC cuts the MAC itself from 1,496 to 1,101 ns (crypto_hash_sha256 of the same input is 773 ns, so most of the remaining HMAC cost is the two SHA-256 compressions, which the state copy skips). In a slower, noisier run the same pair measured 15,642 -> 7,607 -> 7,189 ns, so the relative saving is at least 22% and possibly more of the auth cost. Where it comes from: `header.byteslice(7, ...)` copy of the token (122 ns, 2 objs), the `.b` copy of the signing input (123 ns, 2 objs), rbnacl's `sodium_function` splat wrappers (hmac 1,534 vs 1,496 direct, verify32 200 vs 155 direct), the BASE64URL regex pre-checks on signature and payload (200 + 376 ns, redundant because `unpack1("m0")` is strict), decode64 building a new padded string (513/593 ns, 4 objs each vs 472 / 3 with tr! in place), `Time.now.to_f` 111 ns + 1 obj vs clock_gettime 60 ns + 0. JWT is still fully verified on every request. HMAC alternatives measured and rejected: OpenSSL::HMAC.digest 6,250 ns / 3 objs, OpenSSL::HMAC#reset path 2,203 ns, HMAC#dup path 1,763 ns / 3 objs, OpenSSL::Digest ipad/opad with dup 1,453 ns / 10 objs, Digest::SHA256 ipad/opad 2,959 ns. Only ~7.8% of requests carry a token (0.17 of 2.17 per loop), so -1.2..-1.5 us per authenticated request is about -0.1 us per request overall.
all_proposals.correctness_risk: Keep behaviour for every malformed-token shape: strict m0 decoding raises ArgumentError for any character outside the base64 alphabet or bad padding, which the old regex + decode pair also rejected; a payload whose length is 1 mod 4 must still be rejected (pad == 3 branch above replicates `segment.bytesize % 4 != 1`); the fixed 43-char signature check stays. put_bytes/get_bytes on FFI::MemoryPointer are plain memcpy; the template contains the keyed (ipad/opad) state, never the raw secret in a Ruby object beyond @key, which already exists. Run test/test.sh (the 401 cases) and compare against a few hand-built tokens with wrong alg header, expired exp, non-numeric sub.
all_proposals.rule_risk: none (no memoization of verified tokens; a precomputed keyed state is key material, not a per-request cache)

all_proposals.title: Drop the redundant leading reset on bound statements and prepare BEGIN/COMMIT once
all_proposals.change: In app.rb class Store: `document = @post.bind(id).next; @post.reset` (and likewise `@create.bind(...).next` / `@exists.bind(post_id).next`) instead of `@x.reset.bind(...).next; @x.reset` -- keep the trailing reset. Leave `@feed.reset.next; @feed.reset` as is (no measurable gain for an unbound statement). Prepare `@begin = @db.prepare("BEGIN IMMEDIATE")`, `@commit = @db.prepare("COMMIT")` (and ROLLBACK) in initialize and call `.execute` on them instead of `@db.execute("BEGIN IMMEDIATE")`/`@db.execute("COMMIT")`. (Already folded into group-commit-leader-fiber; listed separately in case that one is not taken.)
all_proposals.rationale: extralite's Query#bind sets should_reset, and Query_perform_next calls query_reset (sqlite3_reset + the pre-query hook) before stepping, so `reset.bind.next` resets the statement twice. Measured: `@post.reset.bind(id).next; @post.reset` 1,846 ns vs `@post.bind(id).next; @post.reset` 1,737 ns (-110 ns, 6% of the post lookup) on a request that is 46% of the mix (~0.05 us per request). `@db.execute("BEGIN IMMEDIATE")` + `@db.execute("COMMIT")` cost 656 ns per batch (statement-cache hash lookups) vs 476 ns with prepared statements (-180 ns per batch, <=170 batches/s: negligible CPU, but free).
all_proposals.correctness_risk: Trailing reset must stay so no statement is left mid-step holding a read transaction (the comment in Store explains why: it would block checkpoints). Otherwise behaviour-neutral.

all_proposals.title: Skip the Unicode TRIM gsub on POST /posts when both end bytes are printable ASCII
all_proposals.change:
In App#create replace `body = body.gsub(TRIM, "")` with:

first = body.getbyte(0); last = body.getbyte(-1)
body = body.gsub(TRIM, "") unless first && first.between?(0x21, 0x7E) && last.between?(0x21, 0x7E)

(empty body: getbyte(0) is nil -> falls through to gsub, then the existing empty check). Everything else in create stays (CODER.load, valid_encoding?, length checks).
all_proposals.rationale: TRIM = /\A[...]+|[...]+\z/ with the JavaScript whitespace set is a Unicode character-class regex whose `\z` alternative is attempted at every position, so gsub costs ~1.8 us for the ~70-char load-test body (and 28 us for a 467-char body) even when there is nothing to trim. Every JS whitespace character is either ASCII 0x09-0x0D/0x20 or a multibyte UTF-8 sequence whose first byte is >= 0xC2 and whose last byte is a continuation byte 0x80-0xBF, so a printable ASCII byte (0x21-0x7E) at both ends proves the string has nothing to trim; the guard measured 0.28 us with String#[] (0 allocations with getbyte). Creates are only 0.02/2.17 = 0.9% of requests, so this is ~0.02% CPU; it mostly trims ~2 us (or far more for long bodies) off POST /posts latency.
all_proposals.correctness_risk: Bytes are identical in every case: gsub still runs whenever either end byte is not printable ASCII (spaces, tabs, NBSP, BOM, any non-ASCII first/last char), so test/test.sh's trimming checks and the 500/501-character checks behave exactly as today.

all_proposals.title: FEED: drop ORDER BY inside group_concat (removes the temp b-tree sorter)
all_proposals.change:
app.rb, `Store::FEED`: replace `group_concat(doc,',' ORDER BY created_at DESC,id DESC)` with `group_concat(doc,',')` and drop the now-unused `p.created_at,p.id` projection from the subquery, i.e.

FEED = "SELECT '{\"posts\":['||coalesce(group_concat(doc,','),'')||']}' FROM (SELECT #{POST_JSON} AS doc FROM posts p JOIN users u ON u.id=p.user_id ORDER BY p.created_at DESC,p.id DESC LIMIT 20)"

Keep the subquery's ORDER BY ... LIMIT 20 exactly as is: SQLite runs it as a CO-ROUTINE over posts_created_at_id_idx (EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows no `USE TEMP B-TREE` any more) and group_concat consumes the rows in co-routine order, so the output bytes are unchanged. Apply the same text to the `feed` statement in sqlite_train.c so the PGO profile covers the new shape. Verify: test/test.sh 42/42 plus a byte-compare of old-vs-new FEED on the seed DB before and after a few hundred mixed likes/posts (done here: identical 5102-byte documents in both states).

Fallback with documented ordering at the same measured cost (23.9 vs 23.2 us): `SELECT doc FROM (same subquery)` as a 20-row splat query (`@feed.reset.to_a`), then in Ruby `'{"posts":[' + rows.join(',') + ']}'`. Choose it if relying on co-routine delivery order is unacceptable to the reviewer.
all_proposals.rationale: FEED is 46% of requests and ~85% of all SQLite time (micro: FEED 31.9 us vs POST 2.3 us, LIKE ~17 us, CREATE ~21 us; weighted ~17 us/req, matching perf's ~15%). The aggregate ORDER BY forces `USE TEMP B-TREE FOR group_concat(ORDER BY)`: OpenEphemeral + 20 sorter inserts + a second pass; opcodes 71 -> 59, VM steps per run 1048 -> 846 (Query#status(VM_STEP)). Measured in tdsc-cicloid:base with --cpus 1 (PGO build): FEED 31.9 -> 23.2 us on the fresh seed, 26-28 -> 17-19 us after writes; in the non-PGO A/B builds 36 -> 26 us. ~8.5 us per feed x 0.46 = ~3.9 us/req of 110.4 us = ~3.5%. temp_store=MEMORY already makes the sorter pure CPU, so this is CPU, not I/O.
all_proposals.correctness_risk: SQLite documents group_concat order without ORDER BY as arbitrary; in practice it is the delivery order of the co-routine, i.e. the subquery's ORDER BY via posts_created_at_id_idx (the only ordered access path, no runtime ANALYZE, so the plan is stable). test.sh checks feed order; add the byte-compare above as a local gate. The Ruby-join fallback has zero ordering risk at the same cost.
all_proposals.rule_risk: none (no caching, schema/indexes untouched, identical response bytes)

all_proposals.title: Group commit via one task.yield, no Async::Promise, no per-batch Task; reads never wait
all_proposals.change:
Rewrite Store's write path (app.rb):
- State: `@pending = []` (entries `[op, slot]`, slot = `[]`), remove `@batch`, `require "async/promise"`, `begin_batch`, `commit`.
- `create(user_id, username, body)` -> `enqueue([:create, user_id, body, username])`; `like(user_id, post_id)` -> `enqueue([:like, user_id, post_id])`.
- `enqueue(op)`: `slot = []; @pending << [op, slot]; Async::Task.current.yield; flush unless slot.frozen?; raise slot[1] if slot[1]; slot[0]`.
- `flush`: `ops, @pending = @pending, []; return if ops.empty?; @db.execute("BEGIN IMMEDIATE"); ops.each { |op, slot| begin; slot[0] = run_op(op); rescue Extralite::Error => e; slot[1] = e; end }; begin; @db.execute("COMMIT"); rescue Extralite::Error => e; @db.execute("ROLLBACK") if @db.transaction_active?; ops.each { |_, s| s[0] = nil; s[1] ||= e }; end; ops.each { |_, s| s.freeze }; checkpoint! if @checkpoint_due`.
- `run_op`: `:like` -> `@like.execute(a, b) == 1 ? :liked : (r = @exists.reset.bind(b).next; @exists.reset; r ? :already_liked : :missing)`; `:create` -> `d = @create.reset.bind(a, b, c).next; @create.reset; d`.
- `feed`/`post`: delete `@batch&.wait` (no transaction is ever open while a reader runs, because BEGIN..COMMIT happens inside one synchronous `flush` with no fiber switch).
- `checkpoint`: `@db.transaction_active? ? @checkpoint_due = true : checkpoint!` (always the latter in practice).
flush must contain no scheduler I/O or yields. Optional second step, only if the full bench shows transactions/s much higher than ~118: when `ops.size == 1` yield once more before flushing to widen batches (WAL frames per like drop from ~4.5 to ~2.2 at 5 per txn).
all_proposals.rationale: Measured under the Async reactor: a pending `Async::Promise#wait` costs ~6-7 us per waiting fiber (Mutex+ConditionVariable+scheduler block/unblock; 17.8 us cold), `Async::Condition` ~5 us, `task.yield` ~1.3 us. Today every writer and every reader that lands in a pass after the first write pays the Promise wait, and every batch spawns an `Async { task.yield; commit }` Task+Fiber. New design: one yield per writer, no Task per batch, no Promise, readers never wait. At 71k users (~589 writes/s, ~118-589 batches/s, a few hundred reader-waiters/s) that is ~4-8 ms of CPU per second out of ~830 ms busy = ~0.5-1%, plus every affected read is answered in the same reactor pass instead of the next (small latency win). Durability semantics are identical: a writer responds only after the COMMIT of the flush that ran its statement.
all_proposals.correctness_risk: LIKE's EXISTS check and CREATE's RETURNING/created_at now execute at flush time (one reactor pass later) - indistinguishable to clients. Statement error -> only that request fails (today the exception also skips the wait and the batch still commits); COMMIT error -> all ops of that flush fail (same as today). Must keep `flush` free of fiber switches. Gate: test.sh 42/42 plus a burst test of concurrent likes/creates including duplicate likes and missing posts.
all_proposals.rule_risk: none: still group commit with each response waiting for its own commit; no state carried across requests

all_proposals.title: PRAGMA mmap_size=0, keep the 64 MiB page cache (avoid per-access btreeInitPage re-parse)
all_proposals.change: app.rb `Store#initialize`: change `@db.execute("PRAGMA mmap_size=1073741824")` to `@db.execute("PRAGMA mmap_size=0")`; keep `PRAGMA cache_size=-65536` (optionally -131072; RSS budget allows). Mirror in sqlite_train.c's pragma string (`PRAGMA mmap_size=0; PRAGMA cache_size=-65536; PRAGMA temp_store=MEMORY;`) so PGO trains the pcache path. Decide by a full-bench A/B (both directions); keep whichever wins.
all_proposals.rationale: With mmap, clean pages are served from the mapping and are not retained in the page cache: every fetch does walFindFrame -> unixFetch -> pagerAcquireMapPage (fresh PgHdr) -> btreeInitPage, which re-parses the page header and cell pointer array on each access. With the pcache the hot page stays parsed (MemPage.isInit) across statements. Same-process micro A/B on the seed DB (--cpus 1, PGO build): FEED -4..-6%, POST -5..-8%, with the WAL both empty and populated -> ~0.6-1 us/req = ~0.5-1%. The hot set (20 newest posts and their 20 authors, right edges of posts_created_at_id_idx and likes_post_id_idx, randomly hit sqlite_autoindex_likes_1 leaves ~30 MB) fits in 64 MiB; DB is 238 MB on a 2 GB box, so no OS page-cache pressure either way.
all_proposals.correctness_risk: None functional. RSS grows by up to ~70 MB as the pcache fills (362 MB -> ~430 MB, far below 2 GB). First touch of a page becomes a 4 KiB read() instead of a page fault; micro-only evidence from arm64 Docker, so a full-bench A/B on the target is mandatory.
all_proposals.rule_risk: none (SQLite page cache is explicitly allowed)

all_proposals.title: Make sqlite_train.c match the server's pragmas, SQL, data size and id distribution
all_proposals.change: sqlite_train.c: (a) extend the pragma exec to `... PRAGMA wal_autocheckpoint=0; PRAGMA mmap_size=<same value as app.rb>; PRAGMA cache_size=-65536; PRAGMA temp_store=MEMORY;`; (b) use the final FEED text from feed-no-sorter; (c) scale the synthetic DB toward the seed (seed: 50,000 users / 500,000 posts / 2,016,005 likes, 238 MB; trainer: 5k/50k/200k) - change the three recursive-CTE bounds to 50000/500000/2000000 and the modulo constants accordingly, keep ANALYZE; (d) pick post ids like the load test does, from the 20 newest posts (`(sqlite3_int64)max_post_id - seed % 20`, tracking max_post_id after each create) for POST and LIKE instead of uniform over all posts; (e) keep the 1:1 feed:post, 1/7 like, 1/49 create mix and the checkpoint every 1000 iterations (~1 s of production writes). Rebuild via install.sh (profile keyed by $work/sqlite3.o path; `-Werror=missing-profile` still guards coverage).
all_proposals.rationale: PGO is already worth ~11% on FEED in this toolchain (non-PGO build with the submitted flags: 36 us; PGO base image: 31.9 us), so profile fidelity matters more than any remaining compile flag. Today the profile is collected without mmap (trains the pcache path while the app runs the mmap path), on a 10x smaller DB (shallower b-trees, different overflow/interior-page branch mix), with uniformly random post ids (cold pages, many likes per post) whereas the real load only ever reads the 20 newest posts (right-edge pages, 2-8 likes each) and never uses the old FEED sorter path once feed-no-sorter lands.
all_proposals.correctness_risk: None at runtime (trainer only). Build time grows by the larger seeding (seconds).

all_proposals.title: Checkpoint every 250 ms instead of 1 s (latency only: caps the reactor stall at ~1/4)
all_proposals.change: server.rb checkpoint task: `sleep 1` -> `sleep 0.25` (Store#checkpoint unchanged, still PASSIVE, still off the commit path). Optional: read the pragma's row (`[busy, log, checkpointed]` via `@db.query_single`) and log it once a minute to confirm the WAL is being fully checkpointed.
all_proposals.rationale: Measured: 1 s of 71k-user writes = 589 statements / ~118 txns = 2,080-3,350 WAL frames (8-13 MB); the PASSIVE checkpoint of that blocks the single reactor thread 25-47 ms wall (fsync WAL, pread+pwrite per frame, fsync DB) once per second, and the first COMMIT after it costs 0.6-3 ms (WAL restart + header sync). Every request queued during the stall ages by that much, feeding p99. At 250 ms the per-stall work is ~1/4 (and fewer distinct pages per checkpoint), for 3 extra fsync pairs per second (~+1-2 ms CPU/s = -0.1..-0.2% throughput). Pure latency trade: it only matters if p99 (349 ms at 71k) becomes the binding constraint at the target user count.
all_proposals.correctness_risk: none
all_proposals.rule_risk: none (WAL + synchronous=NORMAL unchanged; checkpoint timing does not affect commit durability)

all_proposals.title: THREADSAFE=0 and OMIT_* trims in install.sh SQLITE_FLAGS (hygiene, <=0.3%)
all_proposals.change: install.sh SQLITE_FLAGS: `-DSQLITE_THREADSAFE=2` -> `-DSQLITE_THREADSAFE=0`; remove `-DSQLITE_ENABLE_COLUMN_METADATA` (extralite 3.1.3 never calls sqlite3_column_table_name/origin_name/database_name - grep of ext/extralite/*.c, and the build without it links and runs); add `-DSQLITE_OMIT_DECLTYPE -DSQLITE_OMIT_UTF16 -DSQLITE_OMIT_AUTHORIZATION -DSQLITE_OMIT_TRACE` (none referenced by extralite); with mmap-off-pcache also `-DSQLITE_MAX_MMAP_SIZE=0`. Do NOT add OMIT_PROGRESS_CALLBACK (extralite calls sqlite3_progress_handler in Database init/reset), OMIT_LOAD_EXTENSION (extconf have_func + Database#load_extension) or OMIT_AUTOINIT (would need an FFI sqlite3_initialize before Database.new for no measurable gain). THREADSAFE=0 is safe only because one reactor thread owns the connection with gvl_release_threshold=-1 and the checkpoint timer is an Async task, not a Thread - keep it that way.
all_proposals.rationale: In THREADSAFE=2 the connection mutex is already NULL (allocated only with full mutex), MEMSTATUS=0 removes the mem0 mutex and separateCache gives each pcache a mutex-less PGroup, so the remaining cost is null-checked function-pointer calls. A/B of three non-PGO builds in the same container, fresh DB per run, 3 interleaved rounds: A (submitted flags) FEED 35.9-36.4 us, B (THREADSAFE=0 + OMITs, no COLUMN_METADATA) 35.3-38.4, C (THREADSAFE=0 + COLUMN_METADATA) 36.0-36.5; FEED-no-sorter 25.3-26.6 / 25.1-27.0 / 25.8-27.6; POST 2.44-2.61 / 2.46-2.67 / 2.49-2.71; LIKE x5 txn 47-51 / 46-57 / 48-52 us - all within run-to-run noise. Keep only as hygiene (smaller object, marginally better PGO layout).
all_proposals.correctness_risk: THREADSAFE=0 makes any future use of the connection from a second Ruby thread undefined behaviour (none exists today). COLUMN_METADATA/DECLTYPE removal verified to build and run with extralite 3.1.3 (sqlite3_column_decltype is compiled out; extralite does not call it).

all_proposals.title: Profile-guided Ruby build (two-pass PGO trained on the server's own request path)
all_proposals.change: Replace the single `./configure ... && make && make install` in install.sh (submission install.sh:70) with the two-pass build already written in <repo>/local-bench/variants/rt-pgo/install.sh (lines 72-91) plus the training script ruby_train.rb in the same directory. Pass 1: `./configure --prefix=$work/ruby-instrumented --enable-yjit --with-jemalloc --disable-install-doc --disable-install-rdoc cflags="$NATIVE" XCFLAGS="-fprofile-generate -fprofile-update=atomic -fprofile-dir=$work/rbpgo" LDFLAGS="-fprofile-generate"`, make, make install; install the pinned gems into that prefix (`gem install extralite:3.1.3 -- --with-sqlite3-dir=/opt/sqlite`, then async:2.46.0 io-event:1.22.1 rbnacl:7.1.2 json:3.1.0 ffi:1.17.4); `rm -rf $work/rbpgo`; run `ruby-instrumented/bin/ruby --yjit --yjit-call-threshold=5 ruby_train.rb $work/train-ruby.db` (builds a synthetic DB with the sqlite_train.c schema, forks a 64-connection client, serves 51,200 reactor requests + 18,000 drained in the bench mix: 46% /feed, 46% /posts/:id, 7% like, 1% create; exits normally so .gcda files are flushed); gate `test -n "$(ls -A $work/rbpgo)"`. Pass 2: re-extract the Ruby tarball at the SAME path (profile keys are object paths), `./configure <same flags> --prefix=/opt/ruby XCFLAGS="-fprofile-use -fprofile-partial-training -fprofile-dir=$work/rbpgo -Wno-missing-profile"`, make, make install. XCFLAGS is used only by Ruby's own Makefile (zero references in mkmf.rb), so rbconfig's cflags stay clean and gem extensions built later are unaffected. LDFLAGS (not XLDFLAGS) is required in pass 1 because mkmf link checks for bundled exts link libruby-static and need libgcov. If the harness Dockerfile is used, extend `COPY install.sh sqlite_train.c* /app/` (local-bench/Dockerfile:8) to also copy ruby_train.rb app.rb http.rb epoll.rb; on the droplet the whole directory is present so no change is needed.
all_proposals.rationale: Ruby's C runtime (rb_str_*, hash, GC marking/sweeping, fiber transfer, io_buffer, rb_io_write) is what the YJIT-compiled Ruby calls into for most of the per-request work; PGO reorders hot/cold code and improves inlining/branch layout there. Measured in the local arm64 harness, interleaved n=5 on core 3, 64 keep-alive clients: base min 24.34 / median 25.97 us/req vs rt-pgo min 23.02 / median 24.10 us/req (-1.3 us/req by min, -5.4% of userland CPU; the median gap of -1.9 is inflated by two base outliers at 30.8/31.4). Userland is ~25 of the ~110 us/req total measured in the 20k bench, so -1.3 us is ~1.2% of total CPU/req. Image tdsc-cicloid:rt-pgo; log <scratchpad>/micro/build-rt-pgo.log (training line: 'ruby_train: 51200 reactor requests + 18000 drained'); A/B raw numbers in .../scratchpad/micro/abimg-1793227751.jsonl. The profile gate passed and the final ruby's .text size differs from base (0x4ab4bc vs 0x4cfd3c), consistent with the profile being applied. Official test suite on the PGO image: passed=42 failed=0.
all_proposals.correctness_risk: Low: same Ruby source, -fprofile-partial-training keeps un-profiled code optimised normally, 42/42 tests pass. Install time roughly doubles (two Ruby compiles + a ~1-2 min training run); fits the install.sh budget but verify on the 1-vCPU droplet. Training must exit normally (no exit!) or no profile is written; the gate catches that.
all_proposals.rule_risk: none (build flags only; no caching, no response changes)

all_proposals.title: Replace Async::Promise batch handle with a 2-method Batch class and `loop do` with `while true` (removes YJIT fallbacks and 185k throws per 96k requests)
all_proposals.change: Apply the three edits already made in <repo>/local-bench/variants/rt-yjit-shape/{app.rb,http.rb}. (1) app.rb: add before Store a `class Batch` with `@fibers=[]`, `@outcome=nil`; `wait`: `unless @outcome; @fibers << Fiber.current; Fiber.scheduler.transfer; end; raise @outcome if @outcome.is_a?(Exception); @outcome`; `finish(outcome)`: `@outcome = outcome; scheduler = Fiber.scheduler; @fibers.each { |fiber| scheduler.unblock(nil, fiber) if fiber.alive? }; @fibers.clear`. In begin_batch (app.rb:119) use `batch = @batch = Batch.new`; in commit (app.rb:133/135) use `return batch.finish(error)` and `batch.finish(true)`; callers at app.rb:65/72 keep `@batch&.wait`. (2) http.rb:146 `work`: `loop do ... rescue` -> `while true; begin ... rescue StandardError => error; Console.error(self, error); end; end`. (3) http.rb:167 and :170 `service`: both `loop do` -> `while true` (the existing `break`/`return` statements stay as they are).
all_proposals.rationale: --yjit-stats over 96k requests on the base image: fallback reasons iseq_missing_optional_kw 96,414 and forwarding 81,432 (Async::Promise#wait(...) forwards to wait?(timeout: nil), an optional-kwarg call YJIT cannot compile, hit once per read request that joins a write batch) and num_throw 185k (every `break`/`return` inside a `loop do` block is a throw through a Kernel#loop frame; `while` is a plain jump). With the variant: iseq_missing_optional_kw 12,091, forwarding 2,260, num_throw 24, num_send_dynamic 2.4% -> 0.4%, objects/req 20.6 -> 18.5, GCs per run 53 -> 43-44. Interleaved micro A/B on core 3 (n=5): base min 24.37 / med 25.73 vs shape min 22.25 / med 25.15 us/req; single earlier pair 26.21 vs 24.46 -- about -1 us/req (~4% of userland, ~1% of total CPU/req). Official test suite on image tdsc-cicloid:rt-yjit-shape: 42/42. Stats files: .../scratchpad/micro/yjit-stats-full.txt (base) and yjit-stats-shape.txt; A/B raw: abshape-1793226870.jsonl.
all_proposals.correctness_risk: Low-medium: Batch#wait after finish returns immediately (same as a resolved Promise); exception outcomes re-raise in every waiter exactly as Promise#reject did. Guard `fiber.alive?` in finish so a connection fiber stopped while waiting (shutdown) is not transferred to. Durability is unchanged: waiters are released only after commit's fsync-backed transaction returns.

all_proposals.title: GC heap/malloc limits via environment in start.sh (halves GC count under load, quarters it when idle-heavy)
all_proposals.change: In start.sh, before the final `exec`, add: `export RUBY_GC_HEAP_FREE_SLOTS_GOAL_RATIO=0.6 RUBY_GC_HEAP_FREE_SLOTS_MAX_RATIO=0.9 RUBY_GC_HEAP_FREE_SLOTS_MIN_RATIO=0.4 RUBY_GC_MALLOC_LIMIT=134217728 RUBY_GC_MALLOC_LIMIT_MAX=268435456 RUBY_GC_OLDMALLOC_LIMIT=134217728 RUBY_GC_OLDMALLOC_LIMIT_MAX=536870912 RUBY_GC_HEAP_OLDOBJECT_LIMIT_FACTOR=4.0`. All eight variables are read by Ruby 4.0.7's gc/default (verified by the measured change in GC counts; GC.stat reasons in the harness are minor:newobj, i.e. slot exhaustion, which is exactly what the FREE_SLOTS ratios widen). RUBY_GC_HEAP_INIT_SLOTS is unnecessary because Process.warmup + the startup warm-up already size and compact the heap.
all_proposals.rationale: Measured in the micro harness (core 0, 4 interleaved rounds): GCs per 128k-request run 53 -> 25 with GC share of CPU 2.2% -> 1.8%; with 20k idle connections' buffers resident (closer to the 20k-user bench) 50 -> 13 GCs and 3.6% -> 2.1% of CPU, us/req min 28.76 -> 24.95 (idle case) and 26.52 -> 25.63 (busy case; noisy core). Cost: RSS 208 -> 230-260 MB, fine on the 2 GB droplet. Raw numbers: .../scratchpad/micro/ab-1793225742.jsonl (labels gc_tuned, gc_tuned_idle20k). Net saving is roughly 1-1.5% of userland, i.e. 0.3-1% of total CPU/req; larger when the heap holds many idle-connection buffers.
all_proposals.correctness_risk: None functionally; only memory headroom. Keep RSS under ~600 MB on the droplet (measured peak 260 MB).

all_proposals.title: Build the response head+body with one interpolation instead of String.new(capacity:) + <<
all_proposals.change: http.rb:284-289, replace the body of `respond` with: `write(socket, "#{heads[status] || heads[500]}#{document.bytesize}\r\n\r\n#{document}")`. The head constants are ASCII-only frozen literals and document is UTF-8 JSON, so the interpolated result is UTF-8 and `socket.write` sends the same bytes. END_HEAD stays in use by the parser.
all_proposals.rationale: `String.new(head, capacity: n)` is a cfunc call with keyword arguments: rb_scan_args duplicates the kwargs Hash, so it allocates 3 objects (String + 2 Hash) before the body is even appended; the allocation profile showed 2.0 Hash/req at http.rb:286 plus the `bytesize.to_s` String at :287. Micro-measured on the base image (ruby --yjit, 200k iterations, 1.8 KB body): current idiom 5 objects and 0.93 us per response vs interpolation 2 objects and 0.54 us. That is -0.4 us and -3 objects per request (~15% of the 20.6 objects/req), i.e. ~1.5% of userland and ~0.35% of total CPU/req, plus fewer GCs.
all_proposals.correctness_risk: Very low; identical bytes on the wire. If a non-ASCII head were ever added it must stay ASCII-only or be UTF-8 to keep interpolation encoding-compatible.

all_proposals.title: Build Ruby, gem extensions, SQLite and libsodium without stack-protector/FORTIFY/CET-PAC hardening
all_proposals.change: In install.sh define `NOHARDEN="-fno-stack-protector -U_FORTIFY_SOURCE -fno-stack-clash-protection -fno-plt"`, add `-fcf-protection=none` on x86_64 (`-mbranch-protection=none` on aarch64), then: (a) Ruby configure (install.sh:70) -> `stack_protector=no ./configure --prefix=/opt/ruby --enable-yjit --with-jemalloc --disable-install-doc --disable-install-rdoc --disable-fortify-source cflags="$NATIVE $NOHARDEN"` (cflags, not XCFLAGS, so rbconfig propagates it to extralite/io-event/json/ffi/rbnacl extension builds; `stack_protector=no` is the configure variable that stops Ruby adding -fstack-protector-strong to hardenflags); (b) append `$NOHARDEN` to SQLITE_FLAGS (install.sh:29) so the static SQLite linked into extralite_ext.so loses its 400+ __stack_chk/paciasp sites; (c) libsodium `CFLAGS="-O3 $NATIVE $NOHARDEN"` (install.sh:58). Reference implementation for (a): <repo>/local-bench/variants/rt-flags/install.sh (image tdsc-cicloid:rt-flags). Do not add --disable-pie: Ubuntu's default-PIE toolchain and -fPIC extensions make it unsafe without further -no-pie/-fno-pie plumbing.
all_proposals.rationale: The base image's rbconfig has hardenflags='-mbranch-protection=pac-ret -fstack-protector-strong -U_FORTIFY_SOURCE -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2' baked into cflags, so every Ruby core function and every gem extension carries stack canaries and (on x86_64) endbr64/shadow-stack prologues; the ruby binary has 2,646 __stack_chk_fail references and 6,682 paciasp instructions vs 0 and 2 after the change. Measured on arm64 (interleaved n=5, core 3): base min 23.29 / med 23.90 vs rt-flags min 22.06 / med 23.95 us/req -- within noise, so the gain cannot be demonstrated locally; on x86_64 the removed CET prologues and canaries in rb_str_*, hash and GC paths are typically worth 0.5-1.5% of C-side time. Honest estimate 0-1% of total CPU/req. Raw numbers: .../scratchpad/micro/abimg-1793227039.jsonl; build log build-rt-flags.log.
all_proposals.correctness_risk: Removes memory-safety mitigations from the process (stack canaries, fortified libc calls, CET); no behavioural change. The input parser is Ruby code so the attack surface is the C runtime itself. Verify after the change that `ruby -e 'p RbConfig::CONFIG["cflags"]'` shows the NOHARDEN flags and that extralite_ext.so has no __stack_chk_fail symbol.

all_proposals.title: jemalloc MALLOC_CONF with transparent huge pages for the malloc'd heap
all_proposals.change: In start.sh add `export MALLOC_CONF="thp:always,metadata_thp:always,background_thread:false"` before the exec (jemalloc 5.3.0 from libjemalloc2, verified via ldd /opt/ruby/bin/ruby; the string is accepted without 'Invalid conf' warnings). narenas is irrelevant for this single-threaded reactor and dirty_decay_ms/muzzy_decay_ms changes were measured neutral (je_nopurge label) and cost +50 MB RSS, so leave them default.
all_proposals.rationale: Ruby's object slots live in 64 KiB pages Ruby mmaps itself, but every string over 23 bytes (request buffers, JSON documents, response strings), every Array/Hash backing store, SQLite's page cache and io_uring buffers come from jemalloc. On the 1-vCPU x86_64 droplet with ~200 MB RSS, 2 MB pages cut dTLB misses on that traffic. Measured locally only on the noisy shared core 0 (4 rounds): je_thp min 24.9 / typical 27 vs base min 26.5 / typical 28-30 us/req -- a favourable direction but inside the noise band, and the arm64 Docker VM's THP policy differs from the droplet's, so this needs confirming on x86_64. Honest estimate 0-1% of total CPU/req. Raw numbers: .../scratchpad/micro/ab-1793225742.jsonl (labels je_thp, je_nopurge).
all_proposals.correctness_risk: None functionally. If /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled is 'never' on the droplet the setting is a no-op (it is a process-level madvise, not kernel tuning). Watch RSS: huge pages can add 10-30 MB.
all_proposals.rule_risk: none (process-internal allocator setting; no kernel tuning)

all_proposals.title: Dispatcher reads the request itself (recv_nonblock into the idle worker's buffer) and hands off via a LIFO idle stack; drop the per-request io_uring read
all_proposals.change: http.rb. (1) Replace `@ready = Thread::Queue.new` with `@idle = []` and give each worker an object `Worker = Struct.new(:fiber, :fd, :buf)`; `work(worker)` becomes: `worker.fiber = Fiber.current; worker.buf = String.new(capacity: READ_SIZE); loop { @idle.push(worker); Fiber.scheduler.transfer; service(worker.fd, worker.buf) rescue StandardError => e; Console.error(self, e) }`. (2) In `dispatch`, inside the `Epoll.ready` block for `when IDLE`: `socket = @sockets[fd] or next; worker = @idle.pop || (add_worker; @idle.pop); data = socket.recv_nonblock(READ_SIZE, 0, worker.buf, exception: false)`; if `data == :wait_readable` -> `@idle.push(worker); next` (spurious ET wake-up, state stays IDLE); if `data.nil? || data.empty?` -> `@idle.push(worker); disconnect(fd, socket); next` (recv returns "" at EOF, not nil); otherwise `@state[fd] = BUSY; worker.fd = fd; Fiber.scheduler.push(worker.fiber)`. Wrap the recv in `rescue SystemCallError, IOError` -> disconnect. (3) `service(fd, buf)`: delete the `wait`/`Fiber.scheduler.io_read` branch; first iteration uses `data = buf` (already filled), continuation reads (only when `data.bytesize == READ_SIZE` or state == AGAIN) use `socket.recv_nonblock(READ_SIZE, exception: false)` (recv, not read_nonblock, to avoid the per-IO rbuf the README warns about). Keep the `@partial` prepend logic (`buffer = partial ? partial << buf : buf`); `drain` already returns the tail as a byteslice, so storing it in `@partial` is safe (Ruby COW un-shares `buf` on the next recv). (4) `add_worker`: `@workers += 1; @task.async { work(Worker.new) }` -- the new task runs until it parks in `@idle` and transfers to the loop; the dispatcher is resumed from the ready list next pass exactly as today's `add_worker` behaves. Growth rule: create a worker when `@idle` is empty and `@workers < MAX_WORKERS`. Remove the per-worker `IO::Buffer.new(READ_SIZE)`.
all_proposals.rationale: Per request today: dispatcher decodes the epoll event -> Thread::Queue push (Scheduler#unblock -> selector.push) -> next pass: worker resumed -> Async::Scheduler#io_read (checks io.timeout) -> URing read SQE -> transfer to loop -> next pass: io_uring_enter submits, read completes inline because epoll already told us the bytes are there -> CQE -> transfer back -> IO::Buffer#get_string allocates the String. So the ring read of already-present data buys nothing (there is no optimistic read(2) in io-event for RUBY_FIBER_SCHEDULER_VERSION 3, confirmed in /opt/ruby/include/ruby-4.0.0/ruby/fiber/scheduler.h and uring.c) and costs an SQE/CQE, two fiber transfers and one extra reactor pass per batch (dispatch pass -> read pass -> app/write pass -> write-completion pass). Measured in the image (URing selector, YJIT, --security-opt seccomp=unconfined, 300-byte messages on a ready socket): `Fiber.scheduler.io_read(buf,1,0)+get_string` 1.72 us/op vs `recv_nonblock(8192, 0, buf)` 0.42 us/op vs `read_nonblock(8192, buf)` 0.39 us/op; with 8 KB payloads 4.5 vs 0.95 us. Hand-off microbench mirroring the server (256 workers, 5 jobs per dispatch pass): Thread::Queue FIFO + 2 yields/job = 1.35-1.50 us/job; Array LIFO + scheduler.push/transfer + 2 yields = 1.45 us/job (so Thread::Queue itself is NOT the cost); same with 1 yield = 1.02 us/job. Net per request: ~1.3 us (read path) + ~0.45 us (one fewer yield/pass) + one fewer io_uring_enter per batch of ~5 (~0.3-0.8 us/req on a Xeon with mitigations) = ~2 us of ~111 us. LIFO additionally keeps the hot set to the ~5-10 fibers active per pass instead of rotating all 256 cold stacks (Thread::Queue wakes waiters FIFO -> round robin), which is a cache-locality gain I could not measure locally (0-1%), and it leaves ~246 worker stacks untouched (README: ~70 KB RSS per fiber that ran SQLite).
all_proposals.correctness_risk: Low-medium. Must handle: recv returning "" at EOF (not nil); :wait_readable on spurious ET wake-ups (leave state IDLE, do not disconnect); RDHUP-only events (recv returns "" -> disconnect, same as today); exceptions from recv inside the dispatcher (rescue per fd so one bad socket cannot kill the dispatch fiber); AGAIN state must still trigger a continuation read in the worker; `@partial` tails must not alias `buf` across jobs (byteslice/COW makes this safe, but verify with a request split across two reads in test.sh plus a hand-made partial-header test). The dispatcher now does a syscall per ready fd; if a socket is readable but a worker must be created (add_worker), the dispatcher is suspended one pass as today.

all_proposals.title: Write the response with write_nonblock and fall back to the io_uring path only on partial/EAGAIN
all_proposals.change: http.rb `write(socket, data)`: `n = socket.write_nonblock(data, exception: false); return if n == data.bytesize; n = 0 if n == :wait_writable; socket.write(data.byteslice(n, data.bytesize - n))` (the fallback `IO#write` goes through rb_fiber_scheduler_io_write_memory -> URing io_write, which handles POLLOUT inside the ring). No other change; combine with dispatcher-recv-lifo-workers so a GET is served in a single worker pass with zero fiber switches after the hand-off (passes per batch drop from 3 to 2). A/B this one explicitly at 20k and 60k with the harness (variants: ring write [base], write_nonblock fast path), because the README claims io_uring batching of reads+writes cut CPU 46%->40% at 40k on the target; my local numbers say the write side of that is not where the win was, but the Xeon's syscall entry cost may shift the balance.
all_proposals.rationale: `socket.write` under the scheduler: rb_io_write -> rb_fiber_scheduler_io_write_memory allocates an IO::Buffer wrapper per call -> Async::Scheduler#io_write (Ruby, io.timeout check, ensure) -> URing io_write SQE -> transfer to loop -> submitted next pass -> CQE -> transfer back. The socket send buffer is essentially always empty for a ~1-2 KB response, so the write completes inline inside io_uring_enter anyway; the ring only adds bookkeeping plus a reactor pass. Measured in the image on a loopback TCP pair with a draining peer process, 182-byte writes, 16 concurrent writer fibers (so SQEs batch per enter like production): `socket.write` 1.71 us/op, `write_nonblock` 0.77 us/op, `send(data,0)` 1.32 us/op, `syswrite` 1.49 us/op (syswrite also goes through the ring). Single fiber (no batching): 3.48 vs 1.96 us. Alternative of calling `Fiber.scheduler.io_write` with a reusable IO::Buffer is not viable: io-event's io_write writes `size - offset` bytes of the buffer (uring.c), so an exact-length write needs IO::Buffer#slice, i.e. the same allocation rb_io_write already does. Saving ~0.9 us/request locally plus one io_uring_enter per batch; on the target the syscall is dearer (estimate net 0.5-1.5 us), hence the modest number and low confidence.
all_proposals.correctness_risk: Low. Partial writes and EAGAIN fall back to the existing path, byte-exactness unaffected (test.sh). Slight change in response timing (bytes leave in the worker pass instead of the next pass) only improves latency. Risk is a CPU regression on the target if the ring's amortised submit really is cheaper than a write(2) there; the A/B decides.

all_proposals.title: Serve GET requests inline in the dispatch fiber (no worker hand-off) when no write batch is open; hand off only POSTs, partial requests and GETs that would have to wait
all_proposals.change: Requires dispatcher-recv-lifo-workers and direct-write-fast-path. http.rb `dispatch`, after a successful recv into `worker.buf`: if `data.bytesize < READ_SIZE && @partial[fd].nil? && data.start_with?("GET ") && !@store.batch_open?` (add `def batch_open? = !@batch.nil?` to Store, or expose the predicate through App) then serve inline: `@state[fd] = BUSY; rest = drain(socket, data); if rest.nil? then disconnect(fd, socket) else @partial[fd] = rest unless rest.empty?; @state[fd] = (@state[fd] == AGAIN ? ...) end`, then return the worker to `@idle` without pushing it. If state became AGAIN during the inline service (cannot happen: the dispatcher is the only fiber that sets AGAIN and it is busy serving), simply set IDLE. Everything else (POST, pipelined/partial data, GET while a batch is open, write fallback that would block) takes the existing worker path. If `write` has to fall back to `socket.write` (partial write) the dispatcher yields for one pass; acceptable, or push the remainder to a worker instead for strictness.
all_proposals.rationale: The task asked whether the dispatcher can serve already-readable sockets without a hand-off: for ~83% of traffic (GETs) yes, provided nothing in the path yields. With the two prerequisite changes a GET's path is recv -> parse -> SQLite -> write_nonblock, none of which yields unless `feed` hits `@batch&.wait` (an open group commit from a POST served earlier in the same pass) or the write is partial. Removing the hand-off saves the ready-queue push (xmalloc node), the worker's transfer in and out and the dispatcher's own yield: measured 1.02 us/job for the hand-off+1 yield pattern, so ~1 us/request, and it removes the last worker pass for those requests (batch served entirely inside the poll CQE handler; one io_uring_enter per dispatch pass instead of two). README's negative experience with serving requests from the accept loop was under reconnect saturation and attributed to SQLite running in smaller batches; here the batch is the same set of ready fds the workers would have served in the same order, so that effect should not apply, but it is the reason this is ranked below the two prerequisites and must be A/B'd separately.
all_proposals.correctness_risk: Medium. The dispatcher must never block: guard on batch_open? (reads join `@batch&.wait` today), guard on partial writes, and keep `rescue StandardError` per fd so an app error does not kill dispatch. Keeps the original read-waits-for-open-batch semantics by handing those GETs off instead of skipping the wait. Any exception raised by `drain` while inline must still run `disconnect` and reset state.

all_proposals.title: Group commit with one long-lived committer fiber and an Array of waiting fibers instead of a new Async task + Async::Promise per batch
all_proposals.change: app.rb Store. At startup (inside the reactor, e.g. from server.rb after `server.run(task)` or lazily on first use): `@committer = nil; task.async { @committer = Fiber.current; loop { Fiber.scheduler.transfer; commit! } }`. `begin_batch`: `return @waiters if @waiters; @db.execute("BEGIN IMMEDIATE"); @waiters = []; Fiber.scheduler.push(@committer); @waiters` (push == `task.yield` semantics: the committer runs in the next ready_flush, after every fiber already ready in this pass has joined). Waiting: replace `batch.wait` / `@batch&.wait` with `wait_batch(w)`: `w << Fiber.current; Fiber.scheduler.transfer; raise @commit_error if @commit_error_for(w)` -- simplest is to store the error on the Array itself (`w.instance_variable_set` is slow; use a tiny `Batch = Struct.new(:fibers, :error)`). `commit!`: `batch = @waiters; @waiters = nil; begin @db.execute("COMMIT") rescue Extralite::Error => e; @db.execute("ROLLBACK") if @db.transaction_active?; batch.error = e end; batch.fibers.each { |f| Fiber.scheduler.push(f) }; checkpoint! if @checkpoint_due`. `checkpoint` keeps `if @waiters then @checkpoint_due = true else checkpoint! end`. Delete `Async::Promise` usage and the `Async do |task| task.yield; commit(batch) end` block.
all_proposals.rationale: Every write batch today allocates an Async::Task (Node + Promise with Mutex + ConditionVariable + annotation) and a new Fiber (stack from the pool, ensure/rescue frames) just to run `task.yield; commit`, and every waiter goes through Mutex#synchronize + ConditionVariable#wait (-> Scheduler#block) and broadcast (-> Scheduler#unblock per waiter with selector.wakeup). Measured in the image: `Async { |t| t.yield }` 6.98 us per task; Promise wait across tasks 11.6 us incl. task creation; full pattern '1 writer + 4 readers wait, then commit' = 45.4 us/batch with task+Promise vs 35.6 us/batch with a persistent committer fiber and Array waiters (identical ordering semantics: both are a ready_push that runs next pass), i.e. ~10 us saved per batch plus fewer GC objects. At 71k users (~17% writes, ~600-700 batches/s because batches rarely exceed 1-2 writes at ~5 requests per pass) that is ~6-7 ms/s of CPU, ~0.7% of the request budget, and it shortens the latency-critical POST path by one task creation. Also removes the Promise+Mutex waits of GETs that join an open batch.
all_proposals.correctness_risk: Low-medium. Must preserve: every response for a write waits until after COMMIT returns (durability rule), ROLLBACK + error propagation to all waiters on COMMIT failure, `@checkpoint_due` handling, and the committer must be created inside the reactor before the first request (server warm-up runs before `Async do`, and warm requests do not write, so create it in `run`). The committer fiber must never die: wrap `commit!` in rescue/Console.error.
all_proposals.rule_risk: none (group commit still waits for its commit before any response)

all_proposals.title: Churn regime: when over the connection budget, hand a freshly accepted socket straight to a worker instead of registering it in epoll
all_proposals.change: http.rb `accept_loop`, after `@open += 1; fd = socket.fileno; @sockets[fd] = socket`: `if @open > @budget && (worker = @idle.pop) then @state[fd] = BUSY; socket.timeout = 10; worker.fd = fd; worker.fresh = true; Fiber.scheduler.push(worker.fiber) else @state[fd] = IDLE; Epoll.control(@epfd, Epoll::CTL_ADD, fd, @event) end`. In `service`, when `worker.fresh` (reset it immediately): perform the first read with the existing ring path `length = Fiber.scheduler.io_read(socket, io_buffer_or_slice, 1, 0)` (a ring read that simply completes when the request bytes arrive, usually within one RTT of accept) and then continue exactly as today; the connection is answered with `Connection: close` by `drain` (because `@open > @budget`) and closed, so it never needs the epoll registration. If the socket is still alive after the response (client sent keep-alive and `@open` dropped below budget meanwhile), register it in epoll at that point (`Epoll.control ADD`) before setting IDLE. Count `Connection: close` responses per second in the local harness first to confirm the churn share at the target user count; skip this if the share is below ~10%.
all_proposals.rationale: Above the budget every new connection is served once and closed, yet it still pays: epoll_ctl(ADD) via FFI (~1 us incl. FFI marshalling), an epoll event decode + hand-off in the dispatcher (~0.5 us), and one extra reactor pass before the first read. The ring read on a fresh socket costs the same SQE/CQE as today's first read but needs no readiness pass. Saves ~1.5-2.5 us per churned request. This is different from the README's rejected variant (serving the first request inline in the accept loop, which serialised accepts with SQLite work and shrank SQLite batches): here accept stays a tight loop and workers still run as a batch in the next pass. Requires the Worker struct from dispatcher-recv-lifo-workers (or a Thread::Queue message of [fd, :fresh]).
all_proposals.correctness_risk: Medium. A client that connects and never sends would pin a worker: `socket.timeout = 10` makes Async's io_read wrapper arm a timer (IO::TimeoutError -> rescue -> disconnect); bound the number of fresh hand-offs in flight (e.g. <= 1024) and fall back to epoll beyond that so MAX_WORKERS cannot be exhausted. Must keep `@open` accounting and `disconnect` identical. Only affects behaviour when `@open > @budget`.

all_proposals.title: Shrink the resident worker pool and per-worker buffers (WORKERS 256 -> 64, String buffers instead of IO::Buffer) once workers are LIFO
all_proposals.change: http.rb: `WORKERS = 64` (keep `MAX_WORKERS = 4096` and on-demand growth), per-worker `String.new(capacity: READ_SIZE)` instead of `IO::Buffer.new(READ_SIZE)` (comes for free with dispatcher-recv-lifo-workers), `MAX_EVENTS` can stay 1024 (12 KB buffer, one epoll_wait drains everything). Do not lower READ_SIZE below 8192: requests with a ~200-byte JWT are ~350-450 bytes, but a smaller size would make `data.bytesize == READ_SIZE` continuation reads more likely for POST bodies up to 1 MiB.
all_proposals.rationale: With FIFO Thread::Queue every one of the 256 workers serves requests in rotation, so all 256 fiber stacks get touched (README: ~70 KB RSS each after deep SQLite calls, ~18 MB) and each request runs on a cache-cold stack; 256 x 8 KB IO::Buffers add 2 MB. With a LIFO idle stack only the ~5-15 workers needed per pass are ever used; 64 resident workers cover any realistic pass (writes hold a worker for one extra pass only), and growth to 4096 remains for bursts. The CPU effect is the locality part already counted in dispatcher-recv-lifo-workers; this item is mostly memory (-15 MB RSS of 362 MB) and GC root-marking work (fewer live fibers to scan on major GC). Measured per-primitive costs are tiny (IO::Buffer.new(8192) 1.4 us, only at startup), so the expected CPU gain is small and not separately measurable.
all_proposals.correctness_risk: Low. Growth rule must stay correct (create a worker when idle stack is empty and workers < MAX_WORKERS), otherwise a burst of POSTs waiting on a commit could starve dispatch.

all_proposals.title: Experiment: bounded busy-poll of the reactor for a few microseconds before blocking in io_uring_wait_cqe_timeout
all_proposals.change: server.rb: replace `Async do |task| ... end` with an explicit loop: `scheduler = Async::Scheduler.new; Fiber.set_scheduler(scheduler); scheduler.async { |task| <existing body> }; spin = 0.000020; last = nil; loop { t0 = Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC); scheduler.run_once(0); t1 = Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC); if t1 - t0 > 0.000003 then last = t1 elsif last.nil? || t1 - last > spin then scheduler.run_once(nil); last = nil end }` (run_once(0) is a non-blocking select pass: submit + peek CQEs + ready_flush + timers; run_once(nil) blocks until the next CQE/timer). Gate: first measure voluntary context switches per request at the target load (`grep voluntary_ctxt_switches /proc/<pid>/status` before/after a 60 s window, or `perf stat -e context-switches` in the profiler slot). Only pursue if switches/request > ~0.7; try spin budgets 10, 20, 50 us and compare us/req AND p99.
all_proposals.rationale: When nothing is ready the loop blocks in io_uring_wait_cqe_timeout (without GVL) with the 1 s checkpoint timer as the only deadline, re-arming the eventfd read SQE when needed; the wake-up then pays GVL re-acquire, a cold cache (on a 1-vCPU VPS the host runs other tenants while we sleep) and a full pass. The local baseline shows per-request CPU falling from 110 us/req at 20k users (2.1k req/s, ~1 request per wake-up) to 64 us/req at 60k (6.5k req/s), i.e. a large share of cost is per-wake-up rather than per-request. At the target's 71k users (~4k req/s plus churn, 83% CPU) most arrivals still land on an idle loop, so each avoided sleep/wake cycle saves tens of us; a 20 us spin catches an arrival ~8% of the time at 4k req/s, so the gain is bounded and it burns the 17% idle headroom, which is why the honest estimate is small and could be negative. Pure Ruby, no C.
all_proposals.correctness_risk: Low for correctness (no semantic change); risk is wasted CPU raising p99 at saturation and provider CPU-credit throttling if the VPS is burstable. Keep the spin small and adaptive (disable when the previous blocking wait returned immediately, i.e. the loop is already saturated).

all_proposals.title: Shrink the worker fiber pool back to 256 after bursts (each suspended fiber costs ~1.5 us per minor GC)
all_proposals.change: http.rb: keep WORKERS=256 and MAX_WORKERS=4096 as the burst safety valve, but add a shrink path. In `run` add `@shrink = 0`. In `work`, at the top of the loop before `@waiting += 1`: `if @shrink > 0 then @shrink -= 1; @workers -= 1; return end` (the task ends, its IO::Buffer and fiber stack are freed). Add `def trim_workers; @shrink = [@waiting - WORKERS, 0].max if @workers > WORKERS; end` and call it once per second from the existing 1 s checkpoint task in server.rb (`sleep 1; store.checkpoint; server.trim_workers`). Hysteresis is built in: a worker only exits when at least 256 are already idle, so a burst never thrashes create/destroy. First add a one-line stderr diagnostic (every 10 s or at SIGTERM): `@workers`, `@waiting`, `GC.stat(:minor_gc_count)`, `GC.stat(:time)`; if `@workers` never exceeds ~300 in a 20k run, drop the change. Simpler fallback if shrink is unwanted: lower MAX_WORKERS to 1024 (stale-edge holds are rare in this workload because every request is one segment and the next only arrives after the response).
all_proposals.rationale: Measured in the base image (gc_fibers.rb): minor GC pause 0.5-1.2 ms with 0 fibers, 1.5 ms with 256, 3.4 ms with 1024, 6.9 ms with 4096 suspended fibers (~1.5 us per fiber per minor GC; Fiber/cont T_DATA is write-barrier-unprotected so it is re-marked on every minor GC even when old). 1M short-lived strings triggered 15 minor GCs, so at ~7.5k req/s with ~100 allocations/request expect ~10-15 minor GCs/s: a pool at 4096 costs ~60-100 ms/s (6-9% of the core) versus ~5 ms/s at 256. The pool grows by one worker per dispatched event whenever `@waiting < @ready.size` and never shrinks (http.rb:131,139-150); during an open write batch every reader blocks in `@batch.wait` until the commit at the end of the pass, so any pass with more events than idle workers grows it, and passes get longer exactly when the core saturates. That is a positive feedback loop consistent with the README's knee (156 -> 180 us/req past 54k on half a core). Also a p95/p99 win: the pause of every minor GC drops from ~7 ms to ~1.5 ms.
all_proposals.correctness_risk: Low. Growth path unchanged, so no new starvation mode; only idle workers exit, one per second per surplus. Verify no exception path leaves `@workers`/`@waiting` miscounted (work's rescue keeps the loop). Gain is 0 if the pool never grows on the droplet; the diagnostic settles that in one run.

all_proposals.title: Over budget, prefer closing after /posts/:id and POST responses, not after /feed (29% fewer reconnects)
all_proposals.change: http.rb `drain`: replace `close ||= @open > @budget` with `over = @open - @budget; close ||= over > 0 && (path != FEED_PATH || over > 192)` where `FEED_PATH = "/feed"` (frozen constant; `path` is the already-parsed request target used in `@app.call`). The 192 margin keeps the hard ceiling: budget 65,279 + 192 = 65,471 < EMFILE at ~65,523, so when arrivals outpace non-feed responses the old behaviour resumes. Keep `reject` and HTTP/1.0 paths as they are. Optional refinement with the shed-newcomer proposal: a shed connection stays shed until its first non-/feed response.
all_proposals.rationale: Steady-state churn is a population balance: reconnects/s = (users - budget) / T_off, where T_off is the think time that follows the request after which the connection was closed. From the user model: after /feed 3-7 s (mean 5 s); after /posts/:id 3-8 s then, 83% of the time, straight into the 5-15 s idle (mean 13.8 s); after a POST the 5-15 s idle (mean 10 s). Closing a random served connection gives T_off = 0.46*5 + 0.46*13.8 + 0.08*10 = 9.45 s; never closing after /feed gives 13.2 s, i.e. 29% fewer reconnects: at 80k users churned requests fall from ~18% to ~13% of all requests, at 71k from ~8% to ~6%. Capacity check: closes needed at 80k = 14.7k/13.2 s = 1.1k/s against 0.54*8.5k = 4.6k/s non-feed responses (3.8k vs 5.7k at 100k). Each churned request costs the server roughly +20-60 us (README: 50 -> 69 us/req when fully churned; locally a churned connection is 10 TCP segments instead of 2 per keep-alive request plus accept 6 us + epoll_ctl 3.3 us + close 4 us of Ruby/syscall time), so at 80k this saves ~1-3% of CPU.
all_proposals.correctness_risk: Low: pure keep-alive policy, byte-identical responses. Hard margin guarantees the fd ceiling still holds under any request mix.
all_proposals.rule_risk: Gray under rule 7 (no load-test detection): it is a generic 'keep the connection after a list view, retire after a detail view or a write' heuristic, but it is tuned to the benchmark's user model. Flag it in the README and let the owner decide; no cached or hard-coded responses involved.

all_proposals.title: Send the closing response with MSG_MORE (or TCP_CORK) so the FIN rides on the response segment
all_proposals.change: http.rb: give `write` a flag, `def write(socket, data, last = false); last ? socket.send(data, Socket::MSG_MORE) : socket.write(data); end`, and have `respond` pass `last = heads.equal?(CLOSE)` (respond already receives the heads table; `reject` uses CLOSE too). `drain` then returns nil as today and `disconnect` closes the socket; the kernel flushes the corked bytes together with the FIN in one segment (tcp_send_fin coalesces onto the tail skb). Alternative that keeps the io_uring write path: `socket.setsockopt(Socket::IPPROTO_TCP, Socket::TCP_CORK, 1)` right before the existing `respond` and never uncork; costs one setsockopt syscall instead. `BasicSocket#send` retries through the scheduler on EAGAIN, so partial sends of large /feed bodies are handled; full-MSS segments still leave immediately, MSG_MORE only holds the last partial one until close.
all_proposals.rationale: Measured with /proc/net/snmp TcpOutSegs in the base image (conn_cost.rb, loopback, both sides counted): a keep-alive request is 2 segments; a `write` + `close` connection is 10 segments; `send(MSG_MORE)` + `close` is 8 (response+FIN merged and the client's ACK merged). The droplet profile puts ~40% of samples in the kernel TCP transmit/virtio path, so each segment avoided is real CPU there (loopback CPU numbers are noise-level because the sender also does the receiver's work). fsharp-kestrel measured the same change at -4.6% CPU/req and p99 24.6 -> 18.7 ms at 160k users where ~60% of requests were on shed connections; scaled to cicloid's ~18% churned requests at 80k that is ~1.4%, ~0.6% at 71k. The direct `send` syscall also drops one SQE + completion + fiber switch for that write.
all_proposals.correctness_risk: Low. Bytes on the wire are identical; the load generator reads to the FIN after `Connection: close`, and the FIN now arrives with the body, slightly earlier. Make sure `respond` emits the response in one write (it does: one `out` string).

all_proposals.title: Decide 'shed' at accept time: over budget, queue the new fd straight to a worker and never register it in epoll
all_proposals.change: http.rb: add `SHED = 3` to the connection states. In `accept_loop`, after `@open += 1; @sockets[fd] = socket`: `if @open > @budget then @state[fd] = SHED; @ready.push(fd); add_worker if @waiting < @ready.size && @workers < MAX_WORKERS; else @state[fd] = IDLE; Epoll.control(@epfd, Epoll::CTL_ADD, fd, @event); end`. In `service`, read `shed = @state[fd] == SHED` before the loop sets BUSY and pass it to `drain(socket, buffer, shed)`; in `drain` use `close ||= shed || (@open > @budget + 192)` (the +192 hard margin replaces the current soft rule for kept connections). Nothing else changes: the worker's first read is still `Fiber.scheduler.io_read` (batched with the pass's other reads under io_uring), the response goes through the same group-commit batch, and `disconnect` runs as today. Combine with the FIN/MSG_MORE and endpoint-preference proposals (a shed fd stays shed until its first non-/feed response).
all_proposals.rationale: A churned connection today pays accept (6 us), FFI `Epoll.control` CTL_ADD (3.1-3.6 us measured), one epoll event delivery in the next pass (epoll_wait share, `Epoll.ready` block yield, state lookup, queue push: ~2-4 us) and close (4 us), all for a connection that will serve exactly one request. Skipping registration and the extra reactor pass saves ~6 us of the ~20-60 us churn overhead per churned request (~1% at 80k, 0.5% at 71k) and one reactor pass of latency for that request. Policy-wise, shedding the newcomer instead of a random served connection leaves the reconnect rate unchanged ((users-budget)/T_off either way) but kept users never see `Connection: close`. This is not the README's reverted experiment: that one read and served every new connection's first request inside the accept loop with TCP_DEFER_ACCEPT, which starved the SQLite batches (-13% when saturated); here the fd enters the same `@ready` queue and the same worker/batch path, only above budget. go-epoll-MegaPanchamZ and fsharp-kestrel both use this 'shed at accept' shape (fsharp: shed path skipping its framework was -12% CPU at 160k, mostly framework cost that cicloid does not have).
all_proposals.correctness_risk: Medium-low: the shed fd must be marked BUSY-equivalent so a stray epoll event cannot double-dispatch it (it is never registered, so none can arrive); make sure `@partial`, `@state` and `@open` are cleaned by `disconnect` as today, and that a shed connection whose first request has not fully arrived (partial) is re-read by the same worker (service's AGAIN loop handles this because the fd is never IDLE). Needs the 20k/60k paired bench to confirm it does not reproduce the README's batching regression.

all_proposals.title: Two forked reactors on SO_REUSEPORT to double the fd ceiling (only route to zero churn; likely a wash at 80k)
all_proposals.change: server.rb: after warm-up, `fork` once; each process binds its own listener with SO_REUSEPORT (TCPServer via Socket.new + setsockopt(SOL_SOCKET, SO_REUSEPORT, 1) + bind + listen 65_535), opens its own Extralite connection, and runs the full reactor; parent waits on the child and exits when it dies. Store: drop `locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE` (two connections need the WAL shm), keep WAL + synchronous=NORMAL, set `busy_timeout` ~50 ms, and keep group commit per pass in each process (BEGIN IMMEDIATE contention between the two is the critical path: measure how often it waits). Only one process runs the 1 s checkpoint. Health check unchanged (either process answers). Budget per process stays `soft - 256`, so 130k connections stay keep-alive. Prototype last, after the other proposals; go/no-go by paired 60k and 80k runs.
