all_proposals.rationale: RLIMIT_NOFILE is per process, so two processes hold 2x65,279 keep-alive sockets and the whole churn overhead (3-10% of CPU at 80k, 8-20% at 100k by the per-churned-request estimate) disappears, as the leaderboard footnote notes for entries above 71k. Against it, on one vCPU: two reactors double the per-pass fixed costs (select/io_uring_enter, epoll_wait, timers, GC roots) and halve the per-pass batch sizes that this design relies on (local harness: 110 us/req at 20k vs 64 us/req at 60k, i.e. per-request cost falls with batch size), plus context switches and SQLite lock traffic through the shm instead of EXCLUSIVE mode. The honest expectation is -5% to +5% net at 80k and positive only at 100k+, where CPU is already over budget (71k runs at 83%). Included because it is the only in-rules way past the ceiling without a C extension; io_uring fixed files/multishot (c-iouring-meros, rust-epoll-scooter1337, fsharp's own transport) all need native code.
all_proposals.correctness_risk: High for the effort: write contention and busy waits between two group-committing processes can stall responses; checkpoint ownership; both processes must be healthy within 60 s; memory doubles for Ruby heaps (fine within 2 GB); test.sh must pass against whichever process answers.
all_proposals.rule_risk: none (process-internal; SQLite only, schema fixed, durability unchanged with WAL + synchronous=NORMAL in both processes)

all_proposals.title: Read the request and write the response with direct syscalls instead of io_uring SQEs
all_proposals.change:
File submissions/ruby-async-cicloid/http.rb. (a) Add a class constant `EAGAIN = -Errno::EAGAIN::Errno`. (b) In `service(fd, io_buffer)` delete the `wait` flag and replace the whole `data = if wait ... else socket.read_nonblock(READ_SIZE, exception: false) end` expression with:

    length = Fiber.blocking { io_buffer.read(socket, 1) } # read(2) on the O_NONBLOCK fd: at least 1 byte, up to READ_SIZE
    data = if length.positive? then io_buffer.get_string(0, length)
           elsif length == EAGAIN then :wait_readable
           elsif length.zero? then nil
           else raise SystemCallError.new("read", -length)
           end

The rest of the inner loop is unchanged (`break if data == :wait_readable`, `return disconnect(fd, socket) unless data`, `buffer = buffer ? buffer << data : data`, `break if data.bytesize < READ_SIZE`); re-reads after a full 8 KiB chunk now use the same expression, so `read_nonblock` (and its fcntl) disappears from the hot path. The length argument MUST be 1: IO::Buffer#read treats it as a minimum and `io_buffer.read(socket, READ_SIZE)` consumes the bytes and then returns -EAGAIN. (c) Replace `write`:

    def write(socket, data)
      written = Fiber.blocking { socket.syswrite(data) }
      socket.write(data.byteslice(written..)) if written < data.bytesize # tail via the io_uring path (rare)
    rescue Errno::EAGAIN, Errno::EWOULDBLOCK
      socket.write(data) # send buffer full: let io_uring wait for POLLOUT
    end

`respond` and `reject` keep calling `write`, so response bytes are identical. Do not use write_nonblock (fcntl per call) or IO::Buffer#write (same minimum-length trap as read).
all_proposals.rationale: go, zig, c-h2o and pypy entries all do a plain read()/write() on readiness; cicloid pays an io_uring round trip for both because Ruby 4.0.7 defines RUBY_FIBER_SCHEDULER_VERSION 3 and io-event 1.22.1 only compiles its optimistic direct-syscall path under `#if RUBY_FIBER_SCHEDULER_VERSION >= 4` (uring.c lines 993/1055/1141/1260/1322/1398), so each io_read/io_write = SQE prep + fiber yield + io_uring_enter + CQE dispatch + resume. strace of one keep-alive request: epoll_pwait + 3x io_uring_enter(1 SQE) + 1 wait. Micro-bench under the io_uring selector (arm64, best of 3): read K=1 3.8-4.1 us (io_read) vs 2.6-3.1 us (Fiber.blocking buf.read); write 5102 B K=1 6.86 vs 4.66 us, K=8 6.32 vs 4.90; 60 B K=1 5.46 vs 3.62; full read+write cycle K=1 11.12 vs 9.46 us (-1.7 us, -15% of the I/O path), K=8 8.23 vs 8.13 (-0.1 us, batching already amortises the SQEs). Load runs at about 5.6 requests per reactor pass, so the real saving sits between the two: 0.1-1.7 us of 111 us CPU/req. The 40% kernel TCP transmit cost is untouched. Side benefit: a request no longer needs three reactor passes (read, write, re-queue), which trims p99 queueing at the 71k point.
all_proposals.correctness_risk: Fiber.blocking disables scheduler hooks inside the block; every served socket comes from accept_nonblock (SOCK_NONBLOCK), so a direct read/write cannot block the reactor. The warm-up UNIXSocket pair is blocking, but `far` is drained after each request and responses are <= 5 KiB, so syswrite there never blocks. EAGAIN on read maps to the existing :wait_readable path and the BUSY/AGAIN state machine already covers an edge arriving between the EAGAIN and `@state[fd] = IDLE`. Partial writes and EAGAIN on write fall back to the existing scheduler write, so test/test.sh bytes are unchanged; re-run it (42/42).

all_proposals.title: Serve SQLite pages from a 256 MiB page cache instead of the 1 GiB mmap
all_proposals.change: File submissions/ruby-async-cicloid/app.rb, Store#initialize: change `@db.execute("PRAGMA mmap_size=1073741824")` to `@db.execute("PRAGMA mmap_size=0")` and `@db.execute("PRAGMA cache_size=-65536")` to `@db.execute("PRAGMA cache_size=-262144")` (256 MiB, which holds the whole 238 MB seed database once warm so like inserts never pread a cold page). Nothing else changes; prepared statements and the checkpoint timer are unaffected.
all_proposals.rationale: asm, MegaPanchamZ, zig and F# read through SQLite's own page cache rather than mmap. Paired runs on fresh seed copies (bench_sql.rb, A/B/C/A/B/C, best of 5): feed statement mmap=1GiB/cache=-65536 33.37 and 33.39 us; mmap=0/cache=-262144 30.93 and 32.21 us; mmap=0/cache=-65536 30.41 and 31.69 us, i.e. 4-9% less on the hot feed query (mmap pages go through xFetch/xUnfetch wrappers per page touch, pcache hits are cheaper for a small hot working set; recently written pages come from the WAL via pread anyway with wal_autocheckpoint=0). Counter-evidence: after the bench's like-heavy phase (about 200 likes on each top post) mmap=0 was 3% slower (100.1-100.3 vs 97.4 us), but the load lands likes on posts fetched 6-15 s earlier so the top-20 span stays like-light. SQLite is about 15% of CPU and the feed dominates it, so the net is roughly 0.5-1% in the seed-like state; confirm with a 20k/60k bench before adopting.
all_proposals.correctness_risk: RSS grows by up to about 240 MB (362 -> ~600 MB, limit 2 GB). Cold pages are now pread() into the cache instead of page-faulted; the existing warm-up touches the feed path so the 60 s health budget is unaffected. Query results are identical.
all_proposals.rule_risk: none (the SQLite page cache is explicitly allowed; no rows are cached in the application)

all_proposals.title: One long-lived group-commit fiber instead of a new Async task per write batch
all_proposals.rationale: Every write batch currently runs `Async do |task| task.yield; commit(batch) end`, which allocates an Async::Task and a Fiber and frees its stack afterwards (strace: 500 like requests -> 500 madvise calls, one per batch). Other entries (F#, cpp-eastl, zig) keep a single committer loop. Micro-bench under the io_uring reactor: `Async { t.yield; p.resolve }; p.wait` 9.04 us per batch vs persistent committer + Async::Condition 3.60 us (-5.4 us, and that variant still included a yield). At 71k users there are about 590 writes/s and about 0.5 writes per reactor pass, so almost every write is its own batch: ~3 ms CPU per second, about 0.4% of the 83% CPU budget, plus one fewer syscall and no fiber allocation per write. Prepared BEGIN/COMMIT save a further 0.3 us per batch (0.57 -> 0.27 us for the pair). Group-commit semantics are unchanged: each response still waits on its promise, which is resolved only after COMMIT returns.
all_proposals.correctness_risk: Condition#signal with no waiter is a no-op, so the committer must be started before the first write (server.rb order above). If commit raises something other than Extralite::Error the loop would die and later batches would never commit; keep the existing rescue in commit (it already rejects the promise and rolls back) and let the loop continue. Checkpoint timing is unchanged (checkpoint! still runs from commit when due).
all_proposals.rule_risk: none (COMMIT with WAL + synchronous=NORMAL still completes before any response is sent; each response waits for its own batch)

all_proposals.title: Plain VALUES insert for likes, missing post detected by the foreign key instead of an EXISTS subquery
all_proposals.change:
File submissions/ruby-async-cicloid/app.rb. Change `LIKE` to `"INSERT INTO likes(user_id,post_id) VALUES(?1,?2) ON CONFLICT(user_id,post_id) DO NOTHING"` and replace Store#like with:

    def like(user_id, post_id)
      batch = begin_batch
      outcome = @like.execute(user_id, post_id) == 1 ? :liked : :already_liked
      batch.wait
      outcome
    rescue Extralite::Error => error
      raise unless error.message.start_with?("FOREIGN KEY constraint failed") # likes.post_id REFERENCES posts(id), foreign_keys=ON
      :missing
    end

`@exists` and the EXISTS statement can be deleted. Verify the exact message once with `Extralite::Database#execute` on a missing id (SQLite's text for SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_FOREIGNKEY is "FOREIGN KEY constraint failed"); if Extralite exposes the sqlite error code in this version, match on that instead of the message. App#like's 201/200/404 mapping is unchanged.
all_proposals.rationale: MegaPanchamZ and others use a one-row insert with conflict handling. Measured with the submission's SQLite build: new like via the current `INSERT INTO likes ... SELECT ?1,?2 WHERE EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM posts WHERE id=?2) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` 5.84 us vs `VALUES(?1,?2) ON CONFLICT(user_id,post_id) DO NOTHING` 2.76 us (INSERT OR IGNORE is 2.28 us but swallows the FK violation, so it cannot distinguish a missing post); duplicate like 0.97 vs 0.82 us; missing post 1.01 us (EXISTS) vs 2.17 us (FK error raised and rescued) but missing posts do not occur in the load (ids come from the feed). The INSERT ... SELECT form makes SQLite materialise the SELECT with a subquery before inserting, which is where the extra 3 us go. Likes are about 7% of requests: -3.1 us x 0.07 = -0.22 us/req, about 0.2% of CPU, plus one fewer prepared statement to reset on the 0-changes path.
all_proposals.correctness_risk: Relies on the fixed schema's `post_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES posts(id)` and the existing `PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON`; an immediate FK violation aborts only the statement, the batch transaction stays open, so other writes in the same group commit are unaffected. The 404 path is now exception-based; test/test.sh covers it and must stay 42/42. A user_id that does not exist would now also raise (same message) and be reported as a missing post, but user ids come from verified JWTs so this cannot occur for a valid token.

all_proposals.title: Dispatcher re-polls epoll directly while requests keep arriving; io_uring POLL_ADD only when idle
all_proposals.change:
File submissions/ruby-async-cicloid/http.rb and epoll.rb. In `Epoll.ready` return the count: make `ready` the last expression of the method (after the while loop add a line `ready`). Rewrite `dispatch`:

    def dispatch
      poller = IO.for_fd(@epfd, autoclose: false)
      events = Epoll.events(MAX_EVENTS)
      loop do
        count = Epoll.ready(@epfd, events, MAX_EVENTS) do |fd|
          # existing IDLE -> BUSY/push/add_worker and BUSY -> AGAIN body, unchanged
        end
        if count.zero?
          poller.wait_readable # nothing pending: park on the io_uring poll as today
        else
          @task.yield # let this pass's workers run, then epoll_wait(..., 0) again without an SQE
        end
      end
    end

MAX_EVENTS (1024) already bounds one pass. Pairs naturally with direct-syscall-read-write: together they give the readiness-loop + direct-syscall shape of the go/zig/c-h2o entries.
all_proposals.rationale: Today every dispatcher pass is `poller.wait_readable` (an io_uring POLL_ADD SQE on the epoll fd, a CQE and two fiber transfers) followed by `epoll_wait(..., 0)`; strace shows one epoll_pwait plus one io_uring_enter for the poll per keep-alive request in single-connection mode. go, zig, c-h2o and pypy loop on readiness directly and only block when a poll returns nothing. With the change the busy loop is epoll_wait(0) -> yield -> epoll_wait(0) ... and the SQE is issued only when a pass finds no ready descriptor. Cost of one SQE/CQE round trip measured at about 1.2 us (read A vs B at K=1) plus the kernel-side poll wakeup; at 71k users there are about 1.3k passes/s (7.5k req/s at ~5.6 requests/pass), so about 2 ms/s, roughly 0.25% of CPU, more at lower concurrency where passes carry fewer requests. Latency is unchanged or better: a pass no longer waits for an io_uring completion before it can see the next epoll batch.
all_proposals.correctness_risk: `@task.yield` puts the dispatcher at the back of the ready queue, so accept_loop and the checkpoint timer still run between passes; edge-triggered semantics and the IDLE/BUSY/AGAIN state machine are untouched. When load stops the loop parks on wait_readable exactly as before, so there is no busy spin. Epoll.ready's FFI epoll_wait does not release the GVL, same as today.
